What we usually have is one or more samples, and we use the statistics from these samples to estimate the parameters of the population. For these estimates to be reliable, the sample should represent the population well, have a sufficiently large size, and allow us to calculate its standard deviation. A sample size greater than thirty is often considered adequate because, according to the Central Limit Theorem, this is usually enough for the distribution of the sample mean to resemble a normal distribution for many real-world datasets. This is not a strict rule, but it is a practical guideline, and in general a larger sample is better.

If we want to find the mean of the population, we calculate the mean of the sample and use it as an estimate. To check how accurate this estimate is, one approach is to take many samples, for example one hundred, and calculate the mean for each. We can then plot a probability distribution of these means so that the total area under the curve is one. The range around the centre that contains 95% of the area is the 95% confidence interval, meaning we can be 95%  confident that the true population mean lies within it.

In practice, we rarely have many samples and it is not recommended to split one sample into smaller ones, as this reduces the size of each. When we have only one sample, we calculate its standard deviation and then find the standard error, which for means is the standard deviation divided by the square root of the sample size. The standard error is then used to calculate the confidence interval. As the sample size increases, the standard error becomes smaller, the probability distribution curve becomes narrower, and the confidence interval becomes tighter, increasing the accuracy of the estimate.

If the data is discrete and the sample size is small, we use the Probability Mass Function as the sampling distribution. This allows us to directly calculate the probabilities of events and exact confidence intervals without relying on a continuous approximation. For example, we can look at the PMF and find the smallest symmetric range of probabilities around the expected value, such as 0.4, that contains more than 95 percent of the total probability. The resulting confidence interval will consist of specific discrete values rather than a continuous range, since the statistic can only take certain fixed outcomes.

What a P-Value Is: A Measure of Surprise
At its core, a p-value is a measure of incompatibility between your observed data and a specific statistical model, known as the null hypothesis (H_0). The null hypothesis is a default stance, typically stating that there is no effect, no difference, or no relationship.
Imagine you are testing a new drug to lower blood pressure. The null hypothesis would be that the drug has no effect on blood pressure. You then collect data from a clinical trial.
The p-value answers a very specific question:
If the null hypothesis were true (i.e., the drug is completely useless), what is the probability of observing data that is at least as extreme as what you actually observed?
A small p-value (e.g., 0.03) means that your observed result would be very surprising, it would only happen 3% of the time—if the drug truly had no effect. This "surprise" leads you to doubt the null hypothesis and consider the alternative.
Conversely, a large p-value (e.g., 0.40) indicates that your data is quite compatible with the null hypothesis.

I will first talk about one question posed during class: why is sample size=30 a decently large one? 
It is related to rule of thumb that comes from the Central Limit Theorem (CLT) and historical convention. The CLT says: if you take repeated samples from any population (with finite variance) and compute their means, the sampling distribution of the mean will approach a normal distribution as the sample size grows- even if the original population is not normal. The bigger the sample, the closer the distribution of sample means is 1to normal. In many real-world cases, by around n ≈ 30, the sampling distribution is “normal enough” for hypothesis tests, confidence intervals, etc., to give reasonable results. As n increases, the SE decreases. Around n=30, the variability in estimates becomes much more stable compared to very small samples. Heavy skew/outliers may need more n; if data are already normal, much less can suffice.
Now, I will talk a bit about t-stat, a topic that was just named in the class. In a regression model, the t-statistic is basically asking: Given the noise in my data, is the effect I’m estimating for this predictor big enough to be unlikely just by random chance? It’s a signal-to-noise ratio: Signal is the estimated effect (slope Beta1). Noise is how much that estimate tends to wobble from sample to sample (its standard error) For one-sample mean test: t= (sample mean-hypothesized population mean)/(sample standard deviation/rootn). 
|t| ≈ 1 → effect is about the same size as the typical noise; no convincing evidence.
Example: You test a new fertilizer and plant growth increases by 1 cm on average, but random variation in growth is also ~1 cm. Hard to say if the fertilizer truly helps.
|t| ≈ 2 → effect is about twice the noise; might be significant at ~5% level (depending on df).
Example: Same fertilizer, but growth increases by 4 cm with random variation of ~2 cm. The signal is stronger relative to noise- now it’s worth paying attention.
|t| > 3 → effect is much larger than noise; strong evidence.
Example: Growth increases by 9 cm, variation ~2 cm — this is a big, clear effect.
Why degrees of freedom matter: With smaller sample sizes, we have fewer degrees of freedom (df), which makes the t-distribution’s tails fatter than the normal distribution. This means the “critical t” for significance is larger, and your effect needs to be stronger to clear that bar. As n increases, the t-distribution approaches the normal (z) distribution, so critical values shrink toward ~1.96 for 95% confidence.
Connection to confidence intervals: A coefficient is significant at the 5% level if its 95% confidence interval excludes zero- this is exactly the same test as checking if ∣t| is greater than the critical value for your df. Both are just two sides of the same inference process.
In multiple regression: The t-stat tests whether a single coefficient is significantly different from zero, controlling for the other variables. The F-statistic from the ANOVA table instead tests whether all coefficients (except the intercept) are zero together. In simple regression, these two tests are mathematically equivalent because F-value= t^2.

When we take repeated representative samples from a population and calculate the sample means, plotting these values produces a distribution centered around the true population mean. This observation is a direct result of the Central Limit Theorem, which states that, regardless of the shape of the original population distribution, the sampling distribution of the mean tends toward normality as the sample size grows. In this context, the standard error of the mean is given by $S_{\bar{x}} = \frac{\sigma}{\sqrt{n}}$, where $n$ is the sample size, $\sigma$ is the population standard deviation, and $S_{\bar{x}}$ quantifies how much variability we expect in sample means. As $n$ increases, the spread of the sampling distribution decreases, improving the precision of our mean estimate. Since $\sigma$ is typically unknown, we often estimate it from the sample standard deviation when the sample is sufficiently large. Understanding $S_{\bar{x}}$ is crucial when we wish to estimate the regression coefficients $\beta_0$ and $\beta_1$ in $\widehat{y}_i = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x_i$ from sample data, because the variability in these estimates tells us whether they are meaningful. If the sampling distribution of $\beta_1$ produces a 95\% confidence interval that contains zero, then we cannot rule out the possibility that the true slope is zero, meaning there may be no real linear relationship between $x$ and $y$. This is why the 95\% confidence interval is so central: for a normally distributed estimator, it marks the range in which the true parameter lies with 95\% probability, and it simultaneously indicates where 95\% of repeated sample estimates will fall. The same concept underlies the calculation of the $p$-value: it is twice the area in the tails of the sampling distribution beyond the observed statistic, $p = 2 \int_{\bar{x}}^{\infty} m(x)\,dx$, where $m(x)$ represents the probability density. A small $p$-value (commonly below 0.05) suggests that the observed estimate is unlikely under the null hypothesis, reinforcing the interpretation of a confidence interval that excludes zero.

When I start analyzing data, for example, looking at the relationship between hours spent studying and final exam scores, I often see a pattern in my sample. I might notice that students who study more tend to get higher scores. But then I have to ask myself the most important question: Is this a real relationship, or did I just get lucky with the group of students I surveyed?
Since I'm only looking at a small sample of all students, it's possible that the trend I see is just a random fluke. This is the exact problem the p-value helps me solve. It’s my tool for checking whether my finding is the real deal or just statistical noise.
To do this, we use a formal process called hypothesis testing, where I set up two competing ideas:
The "Skeptical" Idea (Null Hypothesis, H_0): we start by assuming the most boring possibility, that there’s nothing interesting going on. This is the null hypothesis, which states that in reality, studying has no effect on exam scores. It assumes the true relationship has a slope of zero  and that any pattern we see in my data is a coincidence.
The "Interesting" Idea (Alternative Hypothesis, H_a):It’s called the alternative hypothesis, and it proposes that there is a real connection. It suggests that studying does have a predictable effect on scores, meaning the slope is not zero. My goal is to find enough evidence to support this idea.
So, how do I choose which idea is more believable? This is where the p-value comes in.
The p-value is a probability that answers a very specific question: If the "skeptical" idea were true (that there's no real effect), what's the chance that I would find a relationship in my sample at least as strong as the one I'm seeing now?
To make a final call, I need a "line in the sand." In statistics, this cutoff point is called the significance level (alpha), and it's usually set at 0.05 (or 5%).
If I get a small p-value (≤ 0.05), it’s like a surprising result. It tells me that it would be very rare (less than a 5% chance) to see my data if there were no real effect. The evidence is strong, so I can confidently reject the skeptical null hypothesis. I can conclude my finding is statistically significant, and that hours studied likely has a real impact on exam scores.
If I get a large p-value (> 0.05), it means the pattern I observed could have easily happened by random chance. The evidence is weak. In this case, I fail to reject the null hypothesis. This doesn't prove that studying has no effect, but it means I don't have enough evidence to make a strong claim. I’m left without proof, unable to say for sure that a real relationship exists.

The p-value is a core statistical metric used to determine if an observed result is statistically meaningful or likely due to random chance. It is a central component of hypothesis testing, where we evaluate two competing claims:

​The Null Hypothesis: The default assumption that there is no effect or no difference.

​The Alternative Hypothesis: The claim that an effect or difference exists.
​The p-value quantifies the evidence against the null hypothesis.

​Specifically, the p-value is the probability of observing your sample data, or something more extreme, assuming the null hypothesis is true. A small p-value indicates that your observed result is unlikely to be a product of random chance alone.

​To make a decision, the p-value is compared to a pre-set significance level, typically 0.05.
​If p is less than the significant value, the result is statistically significant, and we reject the null hypothesis.
​If p is greater than the significant value, we fail to reject the null hypothesis due to insufficient evidence.
​
When using the p-value, it is crucial to remember these points:

​- A p-value is not the probability that the null hypothesis is true. It is a measure of evidence against it based on your data.
​- Statistical significance does not equal practical importance. A tiny p-value doesn’t guarantee a large or meaningful effect. Always consider the effect size to understand the magnitude of the finding.
​- Avoid treating 0.05 as a rigid cutoff. A p-value is a continuous measure of evidence; a result of 0.051 is not fundamentally different from 0.049.

​In short, the p-value is a powerful guide for assessing evidence, but it should always be interpreted in the context of the problem and supplemented with other metrics for a complete and robust analysis.

Topic: Meaning and Implications of a Zero Slope in Linear Regression
YourAnalysis:
Analytical Perspective on the Meaning and Implications of a Zero Slope in Linear Regression
1. Conceptual Understanding of Zero Slope
A zero slope in a regression model implies that the estimated regression line is perfectly horizontal. In practical terms, this means that changes in the independent (predictor) variable do not translate into changes in the dependent (response) variable’s mean value. Regardless of how much we vary the predictor, the expected output remains constant.

This is not merely a mathematical property — it’s a signal that the predictor fails to explain any linear variation in the response. From an analytical standpoint, this immediately raises a question: is the absence of a relationship genuine, or is it a result of sampling variability or model limitations?

2. Statistical Testing for Zero Slope
To determine whether the slope is statistically distinguishable from zero, we formulate the hypotheses:

Null hypothesis 𝐻0 :-  𝛽1 = 0 — there is no linear relationship between the predictor and response.
Alternative hypothesis 𝐻𝑎 :- 𝛽1 ≠ 0 — the predictor has a statistically significant linear effect.
The t-test is the standard procedure here, with the test statistic:
t = b1/SE(b1)
where:
𝑏1 = sample slope estimate
𝑆𝐸(𝑏1) = standard error of the slope
A very small p-value (e.g., < 0.05) provides evidence against 𝐻0, suggesting the predictor has a non-zero effect. A large p-value means we cannot confidently rule out zero slope — but note, this is not the same as proving the slope is exactly zero. It simply means the data do not provide strong enough evidence.

3. Interpretation and Business/Scientific Implications
Zero slope accepted (fail to reject 𝐻0)
The predictor variable may be irrelevant in explaining the variation in the response — at least in a linear sense. This could lead to excluding the variable from the model, focusing resources on more informative predictors, or exploring non-linear patterns.

Non-zero slope detected
Every unit change in the predictor is associated, on average, with a 𝛽1 - unit change in the response. This can have significant predictive and explanatory value — for instance, in forecasting demand based on price, or predicting yield based on fertilizer amount.

From a decision-making perspective, rejecting 𝐻0 can justify interventions, resource allocation, or further investment in the variable’s measurement and control.

4. Confidence Intervals as a Diagnostic Tool
While p-values provide binary “reject/not reject” outcomes, confidence intervals (CIs) offer richer insight.
-If the CI for the slope includes zero, the data is consistent with no linear effect.
-If zero is outside the CI, the effect is statistically significant — and the CI bounds also provide an estimate of the magnitude of the relationship, not just its existence.

​5. Model and Assumption Considerations
The interpretation of a zero slope is only valid if regression assumptions hold:

- Linearity — If the true relationship is non-linear, a zero slope in a linear model can be misleading.

- Homoscedasticity — Unequal variance of residuals can distort slope estimates and significance tests.

- Normality of residuals — Especially important for small sample sizes.

- Independence — Violations (e.g., time-series autocorrelation) can make slope tests unreliable.

In real-world applications, a “zero slope” result might reflect model mis-specification rather than the absence of a relationship.
 
6. Cautions with Special Cases
If the regression is forced through the origin (no intercept), slope testing can yield deceptive results. The absence of an intercept can artificially inflate or deflate slope estimates, leading to overconfidence in significance where none exists.

Similarly, in multivariate regression, a slope close to zero for one predictor does not necessarily mean irrelevance — it may be correlated with other predictors, creating multicollinearity that masks its individual effect.

7. Analyst’s Closing Observation
The possibility of a zero slope should never be treated as a purely mechanical statistical test. It is a diagnostic moment in the regression analysis process:

If confirmed, it can streamline the model and sharpen predictive focus.

If rejected, it justifies further exploration and potentially enhances predictive accuracy.

If ambiguous (wide CI, borderline p-value), it invites deeper investigation into data quality, sample size, and potential non-linear relationships.

Ultimately, the slope is not just a number — it’s a bridge between statistical evidence and actionable insight.

YourAnalysis:
Analysis: Q-Q Plot, Jarque-Bera Test, and Gradient Descent

In machine learning and statistics, we often need to check if our data follows certain rules and then decide how to train our models. Three useful ideas here are the Q-Q plot, the Jarque–Bera test, and gradient descent in regression.

A Q-Q plot (Quantile–Quantile plot) is a graph that shows if data is close to a normal distribution (bell-shaped curve). In regression, we check if the errors (residuals) are normal. To make one in Excel, we sort the residuals, calculate their ranks, and then find the expected values of a normal distribution using the formula =NORM.S.INV((i-0.5)/n). If we plot the sorted data against these values and the points lie on a straight line, the data is roughly normal. If the points bend away, the data is skewed or has heavy tails.

The Jarque–Bera (JB) test is a more mathematical way to check the same thing. It uses two measures:

Skewness (how lopsided the data is)

Kurtosis (how heavy or light the tails are compared to normal)

The JB test gives a number, and if this number is very high (with a small p-value), we reject the idea that the data is normal. If the number is small, the data can be treated as normal. This is mostly used on regression residuals.

For finding the best-fit line in multiple linear regression, we need to calculate the coefficients. One way is the normal equation, but that needs heavy matrix calculations when the dataset is large. A better way for big data is gradient descent. It starts with some values for coefficients and keeps updating them step by step in the direction that reduces the error, until it finds the best solution.

You might ask: why not use the Newton-Raphson method? It does converge faster, but it requires calculating and inverting a second-derivative matrix (called the Hessian), which is very expensive for large data. Gradient descent only uses the first derivative, so it is simpler and works better in practice for machine learning problems.

In short:

Q-Q plots and JB test check if data or residuals are normal.

Gradient descent is preferred in regression with large data because it is simpler and more scalable than Newton-Raphson.

In today’s lecture, we started by running a Python program using the scikit-learn library to perform linear regression on a dataset, which helped us see how machine learning models are built in practice. We then discussed why we can’t just use all our data for both training and testing, since that would lead to overfitting—the model would just “memorize” instead of actually learning. To fix this, we usually split data into training and testing parts (often 80%-20%). We also saw how statisticians check if a model is reliable, using tools like the QQ plot and the Jarque-Bera test, which tell us whether the model errors behave like a normal distribution. After this, we went deeper into the math of regression, starting from simple linear regression (one input variable) to multiple linear regression (many input features), and expressed them neatly using matrices. Finally, we learned about the cost function, which measures how wrong the model is, and how gradient descent is used to gradually adjust the model’s weights step by step until the errors are minimized.

NEWTON-RAPHSON METHOD
The Newton-Raphson method is a step-by-step way to find solutions of equations of the form f(x)=0. It starts with an initial guess and then improves it by using the function’s value and its slope (first derivative) at that point. At each step, we draw a tangent to the curve and see where it crosses the x-axis; that crossing becomes the new guess. Repeating this process usually brings us very close to the actual root. This gives the method more accurate steps compared to just using the slope alone, which is why Newton’s method can converge much faster than gradient descent.

Now, when we use Newton-Raphson for optimization problems (like in machine learning), the goal is to find where the slope is zero, i.e., solve f′(x)=0. Applying Newton-Raphson to the derivative introduces the second derivative (curvature). 

When we compare this with gradient descent, both methods involve taking steps to reach a solution, but they differ in approach. Gradient descent is more general and only needs the first derivative; it takes small steps in the opposite direction of the slope to slowly reduce the error. Newton-Raphson, on the other hand, also uses the second derivative (curvature information), which often allows it to converge much faster, sometimes in just a few steps. However, this speed comes at the cost of complexity—calculating second derivatives can be heavy or impractical in large machine learning problems. That’s why gradient descent is more commonly used in ML, while Newton-Raphson is often used in math and optimization problems where the function is simpler and derivatives are easier to compute.

The Jarque-Bera (JB) test is a widely used statistical test for assessing whether a dataset, or more specifically the residuals of a regression model, follow a normal distribution. Normality is a key assumption in many statistical methods, including linear regression, hypothesis testing, because it underpins the validity of confidence intervals and significance tests. The JB test is based on two critical characteristics of a distribution: skewness and kurtosis. Skewness measures the degree of asymmetry in the data, while kurtosis reflects the “tailedness” or the extent of extreme values. For a perfectly normal distribution, skewness should be close to zero and kurtosis close to three. The Jarque-Bera statistic is calculated using these two measures, and under the null hypothesis of normality, it follows a chi-squared distribution with two degrees of freedom.
Interpretation is straightforward:
A low JB statistic with a high p-value (> 0.05) suggests that the residuals are consistent with normality, meaning the assumption holds.
A high JB statistic with a low p-value (< 0.05) indicates that the data significantly deviate from normality, often due to skewness, heavy tails, or outliers.
One strength of the test is its simplicity and reliance on fundamental distribution properties. However, it has limitations. For small sample sizes, the test may lack power, failing to detect non-normality. In large datasets, even minor deviations may appear statistically significant.
Overall, the Jarque-Bera test is a practical and effective tool for diagnosing normality, especially when used alongside visual methods like the QQ plot.

Topic: MODEL DIAGNOSTICS AND SELECTION IN STATISTICS
YourAnalysis:
Statistical modeling involves not only fitting models but also checking whether they are appropriate. This analysis looks at key tools for diagnosing model assumptions and choosing between models: Q–Q plots, the Jarque–Bera test, and information criteria (AIC and BIC).

The Need for Model Evaluation

Statistical models rely on certain assumptions. For example, linear regression assumes that residuals are normally distributed, have constant variance, and are independent. Time-series models assume stationarity and particular error patterns. While violations of these assumptions do not always invalidate a model, they can change how results should be interpreted.

In practice, analysts rarely stick with one model. Instead, they compare multiple models with different levels of complexity. The goal is to balance fit with simplicity. Without proper diagnostic tools and selection criteria, modeling risks turning into mere curve-fitting, which often leads to overfitting and poor performance on new data.

Visual Assessment: Q–Q Plots

Q–Q plots compare a sample distribution to a theoretical distribution by plotting sample quantiles against theoretical quantiles. If the two match, the points fall along a 45-degree line. Curved patterns suggest skewness, S-shaped patterns suggest heavy tails, and flat patterns suggest light tails.

Q–Q plots are useful because they give quick visual insight into how distributions differ from normality. They are especially valuable with small samples, where they help separate random variation from systematic patterns. However, interpretation can be subjective, and Q–Q plots do not provide formal thresholds.

Formal Testing: Jarque–Bera

The Jarque–Bera (JB) test provides a formal way to check normality using skewness and kurtosis. For a normal distribution, skewness should be zero and kurtosis should be three. The JB test statistic measures how far these values are from the expected ones and compares it to a chi-square distribution with two degrees of freedom.

Large JB values with small p-values signal significant departures from normality. This is especially important in regression, where many methods rely on normal error terms. The test offers a clear decision rule, but it has weaknesses: it is sensitive to sample size and only checks skewness and kurtosis, ignoring other possible deviations.

Model Selection: AIC and BIC

Information criteria help in choosing between models by combining fit with a penalty for complexity:

AIC = −2ln(L) + 2k

BIC = −2ln(L) + k ln(n)

where L is the likelihood, k is the number of parameters, and n is the sample size. Lower values suggest a better balance of fit and simplicity.

AIC, based on information theory, focuses on predictive accuracy. BIC, based on Bayesian ideas, applies a stronger penalty for complexity and is better suited for identifying the most likely true model. Both are relative measures and assume that the set of candidate models is reasonable.

Integrated Use and Limitations

These tools work best when used together rather than alone. Q–Q plots give intuitive visual checks but rely on subjective judgment. The JB test adds statistical rigor but may mislead with very small or very large samples. AIC helps in predictive contexts but may lean toward overly complex models. BIC is stricter but risks excluding useful complexity.

A good approach combines visual checks, statistical tests, and information criteria. No single method should control the decision. Instead, these tools help answer two key questions: (1) Do the model assumptions seem reasonable? (2) Which model explains the data well without adding unnecessary complexity?

Conclusion

Model diagnostics and selection are essential for responsible statistical practice. Q–Q plots, the Jarque–Bera test, AIC, and BIC each provide useful but limited insights. Their real value lies in guiding careful decisions that blend statistical evidence with subject knowledge. The aim of statistical modeling is not to find a perfect model but to develop robust, interpretable models that fit the purpose of the analysis.

Topic: Akaike Information Criterion (AIC) and Bayesian Information Criterion (BIC)
YourAnalysis:
The Akaike Information Criterion (AIC) and the Bayesian Information Criterion (BIC) are methods used for model selection. When several models are estimated on the same dataset, these measures help decide which one strikes the best balance between fit (how well the model explains the data) and complexity (how many parameters it uses).
Both criteria are calculated using the likelihood of the model and a penalty for the number of parameters. A model with more parameters will generally fit the data better, but it may also overfit, capturing random noise rather than true patterns. AIC and BIC correct for this by adding a penalty: AIC uses a mild penalty, while BIC uses a stronger one that increases with sample size.
The interpretation is the lower the AIC or BIC, the better the model. A lower value means that the model has achieved a good fit without being unnecessarily complex. Importantly, the actual values are not meaningful by themselves; they are only useful in comparison. Among competing models, the one with the lowest AIC or BIC is considered the best choice according to that criterion. A lower AIC/BIC value means the model achieves a higher likelihood (fits the data better) and it does so with fewer parameters or with parameters that justify their inclusion.

Topic: Size of Training and Test Dataset
YourAnalysis:
For any given population, we tend to prepare a model trained with a sample, representative of the population over which the model is to be assessed too. But for a given sample, what should be the size of the training  or test dataset ?
If the model is trained over whole sample, then there is no point in evaluating it over the same sample, since it has seen all the data. This can lead to overfitting where the model knows the test data so well that it has even analyzed the noise and irrelevant details within the dataset incorporating potential bias too. For such a case, it has excellent performance on the testing data but poor performance on new, unseen data. 
If the training dataset is small, the model may not be able to capture the pattern within the data accurately which can lead underfitting. Underfitting occurs when a model is too simple to capture the underlying patterns in the training data, resulting in poor performance on both the training set and new, unseen data.
So, an optimal training data size may be about 70% of the sample for a large enough dataset which can increase to 90% too if the dataset is not large enough but of optimal size requiring more proportion of data to extract the pattern from the given data.

The Durbin-Watson test is basically used in regression to check if the errors (residuals) are linked with each other, i.e., autocorrelation. In simple words, it tells us whether the mistakes our model makes at one point depend on the mistakes it makes later. The value of this test always lies between 0 and 4. A value close to 2 means no autocorrelation (which is ideal). If it is less than 2, it shows positive autocorrelation, meaning the errors move together (like if one error is positive, the next is also positive). If it is greater than 2, it suggests negative autocorrelation, where the errors keep alternating between positive and negative.

This is important because OLS assumes that errors are independent. If this assumption is broken, then things like p-values, confidence intervals, and hypothesis tests can become unreliable. For example, say we are predicting monthly electricity consumption. If our model underestimates demand in June, and the same kind of underestimation continues in July due to seasonal trends, that’s positive autocorrelation. If instead, the model overestimates in one month and underestimates in the next, that would be negative autocorrelation.

The Durbin-Watson test acts like a first check to spot this issue. If strong autocorrelation is found, we may need to use different approaches like generalized least squares or time-series models (ARIMA) that are designed to handle such situations better.

Topic: Why does lower values of statistical terms AIC and BIC show that the model is better?
YourAnalysis:
To answer this question, let's start by seeing what log likelihood means. The likelihood function measures how probable the observed data is, given a model and its parameters.
The logarithmn of the likelihood function is called the log likelihood function (denoted by ℓ). Higher ℓ means that the model explains the data better. But if we only maximize log-likelihood, we’ll always end up choosing the most complicated model (for example, by adding more parameters).

To avoid this, AIC (Akaike information criterion) and BIC (Bayesian Information Criterion) are used. These add penalties for more complexity. Their respective formulas are as below.

AIC balances fit (via log-likelihood) and complexity (via number of parameters).
AIC=2k−2ℓ
BIC is similar to AIC, but penalizes complexity more heavily (especially when sample size n is large)
BIC=kln(n)−2ℓ
Here k is the number of parameters, n is the sample size and ℓ is the log likelihood.
We can see that both AIC and BIC attempt to balance a model by taking into account the probability of observed data (through log likelihood) and its complexity (through k and n).
Lower AIC/BIC values imply the best balance between both of these things. 

To further understand, let's say we were to add parameters; then log-likelihood would always increase as the fit improves.
But penalty also increases: For AIC, it grows linearly in k, while for BIC it grows like k ln(n)
Thus, if new parameters truly improve the model, the gain in log-likelihood will outweigh the penalty and thus AIC/BIC decreases; whereas If new parameters just fit noise, improvement in log-likelihood is small, but penalty dominates and hence AIC/BIC increases.

Thus, lower AIC/BIC values indicate that a model achieves the best compromise between goodness of fit and parsimony, avoiding both underfitting and overfitting

Topic: Why Gradient Descent is Needed in Regression
YourAnalysis: When dealing with regression problems, the goal is to adjust model parameters to keep a chosen loss function as small as possible, and closed-form solutions via matrix algebra are available in cases like linear regression. Yet, practical difficulties arise: if the matrix to be inverted is nearly singular, or if it's exceptionally large, the straightforward calculation either hits a mathematical wall or consumes prohibitive computational resources. Columns of a matrix become linearly dependent when at least one feature is a weighted combination of others, rendering redundancy or high collinearity. As a result, the determinant vanishes, and no inverse is available. Here comes gradient descent as a suitable alternative. The method is iterative rather than direct, we begin with arbitrary initial guess values, and each round we adjust the parameters by a small amount in the direction opposite the loss function’s gradient. The gradient, in effect, indicates the steepest rise, so moving in the opposite direction progressively shrinks the loss until we arrive at a local minimum. The proportion of the update is dictated by a hyperparameter we call the learning rate. If the learning rate is small, each update is modest, so convergence stretches out. If the learning rate is large, the updates become oversized and the method can swing past the minimum and oscillate, or worse, diverge entirely. This method is far more scalable and remains applicable even when a straightforward analytical solution is unavailable, establishing it as a core technique within the discipline

Gradient descent works iteratively by starting with random coefficients and updating them using the rule:
βnew​=βold​−η∇J(β)
 
Here, J(β) represents the cost function(J=SSE/2m ​, m is the no. of training examples) and ∇J(β) is the gradient, which gives the slope of the cost function with respect to each parameter. In real-world applications of Machine Learning and Data Science, we are often presented with data and need to figure out how to model it. This involves choosing among the vast multitude of machine learning algorithms. While intuition and trial and error are possible ways to approach this problem, statistical bests like the AIC and its counterpart, the BIC, offer a more elegant solution to choosing the best model.

These metrics reward goodness of fit but penalise model complexity. Complex models may have better fits, but come with the risk of overfitting. Similarly, simple models behave oppositely. This is where these statistical metrics come into the picture.

AIC (Akaike Information Criteria) = 2k - 2ln(L): It estimates lost information. A model with the minimum information lost is invariably a better model.
k is the number of parameters in the model; the more parameters (and the more complex the model is), the greater the AIC score.
L is the likelihood of the model. A higher likelihood (and hence a better fit) results in a smaller AIC score.

BIC (Bayesian Information Criteria) = ln(n)k - 2ln(L): It is similar to the AIC, with a critical difference in the penalty term. ln(n)k is the penalty term, instead of multiplying by 2.

The only difference between these tests is the penalty term. Since ln(n) is usually larger than 2 for most datasets, BIC has a higher penalty for adding more parameters and favours simpler models. The absolute values of the AIC and BIC aren't very relevant. We use them relatively to compare different models fitted on the same dataset.

Log-Likelihood
Log-likelihood measures how likely it is that the observed data would be generated by a particular statistical model.
It is the natural logarithm of the likelihood function, used as a measure of model fit. The higher the log-likelihood, the better the model explains the observed data.
AIC (Akaike Information Criterion)
AIC is a criterion for model selection among a set of models for the data.
It is defined as:
AIC=2k−2ln⁡(L^)
where 
k is the number of parameters and 
L^ is the maximum value of the likelihood function for the model.
Purpose: AIC balances model fit and complexity; it penalizes models with more parameters to avoid overfitting. Lower AIC values indicate a better model.
BIC (Bayesian Information Criterion)
BIC is another model selection criterion based on the likelihood function, similar to AIC but with a stronger penalty for models with more parameters.
It is defined as:
BIC=k*ln⁡(n)−2ln⁡(L^)
where 
n is the sample size, 
k is the number of parameters, and 
L^ is the maximized likelihood.
Purpose: Like AIC, BIC aims to select models that are both accurate and parsimonious. However, BIC penalizes larger models more heavily, so it tends to favor simpler models, especially as the sample size increases.

Jarque-Bera Test
The Jarque-Bera test is a statistical test used to determine whether a dataset follows a normal distribution by examining two key properties: skewness (asymmetry) and kurtosis (peakedness). So basically it tests if the sample data have skewness and kurtosis matching those of a normal distribution. For a normal distribution, skewness should be zero and kurtosis should be three. We take null hypotheses such that data is normally distributed and alternative hypotheses in which it is not. We use JB statistics
JB = n/6(S^2 + ((K-3)^2)/4) where n = number of observations, S= sample skewness and K= sample kurtosis. JB statistics follows chi-squared distribution in which the data is not normally distributed and mostly rightly skewed. 
Interpretation of results :- 
High p-value (typically > 0.05): Fail to reject the null hypothesis. The data may be normally distributed
Low p-value (typically < 0.05): Reject the null hypothesis. The data significantly deviates from normality
Limitations:-
It is sensitive to sample size, May have insufficient power in small samples, but can flag trivial departures in very large samples. In small samples, the chi-squared approximation may be unreliable. 
It assumes that observations are independent, and inappropriate for autocorrelated data. 
It indicates non-normality but doesn't specify the type of deviation

Quantiles are values that divide a dataset into intervals containing 4 equal proportions of the data.
A Q-Q plot creates a scatter plot by:

Calculating corresponding quantiles for each dataset
Plotting quantiles from the first dataset (x-axis) against quantiles from the second dataset (y-axis)
Adding a reference line representing perfect agreement between distributions

Topic: What is AIC and BIC? Are higher or lower values of AIC better?
YourAnalysis:
In the context of regression, evaluation of model performance cannot just rely just on measures like R², since they tend to increase as more predictors are added, even if those predictors do not meaningfully contribute to the model and to avoid overfitting. Hence, information criteria such as the Akaike Information Criterion (AIC) and the Bayesian Information Criterion (BIC) are brought in. Both of these metrics attempt to establish a balance between the quality of the model fit and the complexity of the model.

The Akaike Information Criterion (AIC) is defined as:

AIC = 2k - 2 * ln(L)

Here, k is the number of estimated parameters in the model, and L is the maximized likelihood of the fitted model. The first term discourages overfitting by penalizing the number of parameters and the second term measures how well the model fits. A lower AIC value means the model is considered better since it shows a good balance between fit and simplicity. AIC is usually more forgiving when adding variables, so it works well when the aim is to improve predictive accuracy rather than finding the true underlying model.

On the other hand, the Bayesian Information Criterion (BIC) is defined as:

BIC = k * ln(n) - 2 * ln(L)

In this formula, n represents the number of observations. Like AIC, BIC also penalizes model complexity, but this penalty grows with sample size since it uses ln(n). Therefore, BIC weighs additional predictors more heavily than AIC, especially in larger datasets. Lower BIC values also indicate a better model. However, because it has a stronger penalty for complexity, BIC tends to prefer simpler models and is better suited for finding the true model structure.

In practice, both AIC and BIC are helpful for selecting models. If maximizing predictive performance is the main aim, AIC is often the better choice since it is less strict about complexity. If the aim is to identify the simplest model that explains the data, BIC offers a more cautious standard. It’s important to remember that both criteria are relative measures; they are more useful for comparing models than for interpreting their values separately.

Gradient descent is an optimisation algorithm/process used to determine the best parameters for a model. For multiple linear regression, it is used to find out value of β, where β is used to find the prediction value (Ŷ) which is Xβ. 
The model is taken as Y = Xβ + E, where E is the vector of errors, X is the matrix of independent variables/features & Y is the vector of actual values. 
y_1 = β_0 + sigma(β_k*x_k1) + e_1 ; x_k1 cause we have multiple values of the feature x_1 in different rows. If we have a tabular data for training, x_ji denotes the value of the jth feature in the ith row. 
The idea here again is the same, minimise the sum of squared errors. In the matrix form, this is E^T.E (E^T is transpose of vector of errors). E is Y - Ŷ. Now as Ŷ = Xβ ,E becomes Y - Xβ. E^T.E = (Y-Xβ)^T.(Y-Xβ) 
We define J as cost function = 1/2m * (E^T.E) (where m is the total number of observations). Our goal is to minimise the cost function wrt β (effectively minimising the sum of squared errors). dJ/dβ = (1/2m) * (Y^T.Y - Y^T.Xβ - β^TX^T.Y + β^TX^T.Xβ). On simplifying, we get dJ/dβ = (1/m) * (X^T)(Ŷ-Y). 
The process for gradient descent involves choosing a value for β. From that we calculate the value of Ŷ using Xβ. We find dJ/dβ using the above given expression. Then as our goal is to find an optimal β for our model, we assume a β_new = β_old - n*dJ/dβ ; where "n" is a small number. An appropriate number for "n" is needed. Using a large "n" may cause the model to overshoot the minimum {optimal value for β}. Using a small "n" may require us to have many iterations. 
Using this the values of β are constantly updated. We reach an optimal value of β when we see that the absolute value of β_new - β_old reaches a certain threshold value which is very small. 
The reason this happens is because the cost function is a convex parabola and our goal is to find the value of β that corresponds to the bottom(minima) of the graph. The most optimal value of β is when the gradient of the cost function is 0. When we start with the process of gradient descent, the value of dJ/dβ is large and updating the value of β approaches closer to the optimal value of β. As the process goes on/repeats, the slope becomes more smaller and the changes in β are smaller in size and slowly approaches the optimal value for β. We choose a threshold value as it is not always possible to have the gradient to be 0, but it is practically possible to have the gradient very close to 0.

Topic: How to decide training and test sets from a sample dataset
YourAnalysis:
When building AI/ML models, we need to evaluate their ability to generalize to unseen data. So we split the dataset into :
Training set → used to fit the model’s parameters.
Test set → held back to estimate performance on new data.
The validation set is used during training to tune hyperparameters, perform model selection, prevent overfitting, and allow early stopping, ensuring that the test set remains unbiased

The proportion of train vs test depends on the size of the dataset. As the size of dataset increases, the percentage of the data kept for testing can be reduced. There are different methods of splitting the data :
1) Random splitting : 
-The dataset is shuffled randomly and then split into the training and test sets. 
-It works well when the data is i.i.d. ( independent and identically distributed). 
-It is widely used because it is easy to implement in any library. 
-In classification with imbalanced data, random splitting may result in underrepresented classes in the test set.

2) Stratified splitting 
 -It splits the data while preserving the class proportion.  
- It is mostly used in classification. 
- Essential for imbalanced datasets (e.g., fraud detection, medical data)

3) Time based split ( chronological split)
- For sequential/time-series data (for example: daily stock prices, monthly weather records, or hourly website traffic data) → use earlier data for training, later data for testing.
_The unique challenge of time series data is that the order of data points is crucial, as observations typically depend on previous results.
-Mimics real-world forecasting (train on past, predict future).
-Prevents look-ahead bias.
-Less data variety in training if dataset is short.

4) k-fold cross validation
-K-Fold Cross-Validation divides the dataset into “k” equally sized folds, allowing for multiple rounds of training and validation.
-It addresses the challenge of effectively evaluating model performance with limited data by making the most of the available samples.
-The method divides the dataset into “k” equally sized subsets, trains on k-1 subsets and tests on the remaining.
-Uses all the data for training and testing at different times.
-Reduces variance in evaluation
-Provides stable estimates
-Computationally expensive (requires training model k times).
-Not ideal for very large datasets.
-After completing k iterations, the evaluation results are averaged to offer a more stable and representative estimate of model performance, reducing the impact of data partitioning on overall evaluation.

5) Leave-One-Out Cross-Validation
-It can be considered as an extreme case of k fold cross validation.
-Here, each test set has just 1 sample.
-In this method, each of the N samples is taken as a test sample, while the remaining N-1 samples serve as the training set.
-It is suitable for very small datasets.
-This process is repeated for each sample, resulting in N classifiers and N test results.
-The performance of the model is then assessed by averaging these N results.
-Very slow(requires training model n times)

Both k-fold and Leave-One-Out Cross Validation are preferred for small datasets to maximize data usage.

k-fold Cross Validation and stratified splitting can be combined to produce stratified k-fold cross validation which handles imbalanced datasets better than normal k-fold cv, but it is more complex to implement and computationally expensive.
Conclusion: The choice of splitting method depends on dataset type, size, and task. Correct splitting ensures reliable evaluation and robust generalization.

Topic: Analysing Different Normal Distribution Tests - QQ Plot, JB Test, Omnibus Statistic
YourAnalysis:
Implementing regression on code follows a similar process to that on Excel. Before we start, we must import the required libraries - numpy for advanced arithmetic operations on multiple dimensions, pandas for handling arrays and matrices, matplotlib for plotting graphs, and scikit-learn - the library responsible for performing regression. We use its functions and metrics to prepare and analyse our model.

scikit-learn has a function known as LinearRegression - which returns a model on which we fit our dependent and independent variable to get our predicted values. We further use metrics to calculate SSE, MSE, MAE and R^2 to analyse this data, along with observing graphs. One of these plots which are of particular interest is known as the Quantile Quantile Plot or the QQ Plot.

QQ Plot:
A major question we often have when dealing with errors is: are the errors NORMALLY DISTRIBUTED? To visualise this, we use a QQ plot. We deal with two parameters - Data Quantiles and Normal Quantiles. If we have, for example, m errors, then we distribute the error dataset into m quantiles. We also create equal probability distributions with the same number of quantiles on a normal distribution.

Now, we plot them against one another. If it is a normal distribution, it will be a straight line, since the quantiles will be distributed on both normal quantiles and the error quantiles in the same manner. If not, then there is deviation. Points at the ends, if deviating, show a heavy-tailed distribution or lighter-tailed distribution, and curved patterns show skewness. This is a very interesting and useful way to analyse normal distribution in errors.

However, if we need to mathematically process this, we need to rely on values more than plots. So there comes a need for additional statistics, which is met with another library known as statsmodels.api. The use case behind this is to use normal distribution tests using numerical analysis. Let’s look at two in detail.

Jarque-Bera Test: It is a test used for analysing large datasets, comparing a distribution with a normal distribution numerically. This uses the kurtosis and skewness values to make comparisons and flags datasets which differ largely from normal distributions.

A normal distribution has a skewness of 0 and a kurtosis of 3.

The value of the JB statistic is proportional to the sum of the square of skewness and the square of half of relative kurtosis (kurtosis - 3); multiplied with the sample size. But this statistic just measures how far our skewness and kurtosis are from a normal distribution. It doesn’t tell us about the significance of the result.

So we take the p-value of this, by comparing it to a distribution of the sum of two squares (or chi-square distribution with two degrees of freedom). The p-value tells us if the JB statistic is far enough to conclude non-normality. This is how the JB statistic is used.

Just like that, we have another statistic called the omnibus statistic.

Omnibus Statistic:
It performs the same task of combining skewness and kurtosis into one overall test for normality.

Once we get skewness and kurtosis, we transform them into Z-scores which have messy formulae, and we sum their squares to get the value of K^2. K^2 is our omnibus statistic. We perform a similar operation of calculating their p-value by comparing it to a chi-square distribution with 2 degrees of freedom. This p-value helps us understand the significance of the non-normality.

If the p-value is less than 0.05, this means it is evidence against normality, and if it is greater than 0.05, it is evidence towards normality.

The purpose of these normality determiners is to have simple mathematical tests which conclusively let us know if our errors are normally distributed or not using a number. It is highly convenient and usable in the future. There are many other possible statistics, but these two in particular can help us numerically understand a QQ plot and make easy judgements, compared to trying to understand a plot in detail.

Multiple Linear Regression (MLR) is an extension of simple linear regression where the dependent variable is predicted using multiple independent variables or features. The model equation is written as:
y(predicted)=β0​+β1​x1​+β2​x2​+⋯+βn​x
	​
The aim is to estimate the coefficients β such that the prediction error, measured using the Sum of Squared Errors (SSE), is minimized. While a closed-form solution exists, it is computationally expensive for large datasets and may face issues like singularities when features are correlated.

To address this, Gradient Descent is often used. It starts with random values of coefficients and iteratively updates them using the rule:
βnew​=βold​−η∇J(β)
Here, J(β) is the cost function (SSE normalized by 2m, where m is the number of training examples), and ∇J(β) is the gradient, which indicates the slope of the cost function with respect to each parameter. By moving in the opposite direction of the slope, the algorithm steadily reduces error.

The learning rate (η) controls the step size: if it is too small, convergence is slow, and if too large, the algorithm may fail to converge. Thus, gradient descent ensures efficient optimization of regression coefficients for large and complex datasets.

Topic: Comparison of Gradient Descent and Newton–Raphson
YourAnalysis:
In class we were taught gradient descent, but the professor briefly mentioned Newton–Raphson as well. Since both are kind of similar in spirit (iterative methods), I thought I’d compare them.

Formulas and a bit of reasoning behind them:

Gradient Descent (GD) for minimizing f(x):
x_new = x_old − η * f’(x_old)

The idea is simple: the derivative tells us the slope. If it’s positive, the function is going up, so we move left. If it’s negative, we move right. The step size η decides how far we go. Too small = very slow, too big = might shoot past the minimum.

Newton–Raphson (NR) for solving f(x) = 0 (finding roots):
x_new = x_old − f(x_old)/f’(x_old)

This comes from drawing a tangent line at the current point and seeing where it cuts the x-axis. It usually converges really fast if you start close enough.

For optimization, we want f’(x) = 0 at minima. So we actually apply NR to f’(x):
x_new = x_old − f’(x_old)/f’’(x_old)
That’s why in optimization, NR needs both the first and second derivatives (slope and curvature).

Example A: Solving x² − 2 = 0 (root is √2 ≈ 1.414)

Newton–Raphson:
f(x) = x² − 2, f’(x) = 2x. Start at x0 = 1.
• x1 = 1 − (−1)/2 = 1.5
• x2 = 1.5 − (0.25)/3 = 1.4167
• x3 ≈ 1.4142 → already very close
Very quick, only 3 steps.

Gradient Descent:
Minimize 0.5*(x² − 2)². Gradient = (x² − 2)(2x). Start x0 = 1, η = 0.125.
• x1 = 1.25
• x2 ≈ 1.387
• x3 ≈ 1.413
• x4 ≈ 1.41421 (very close)
Took 4 steps, so slower than NR.

Divergence note: If η = 0.5, GD oscillates between 2 and −2 forever.

So here NR is clearly faster. 

Example B: Root of f(x) = x^(1/3)

Newton–Raphson:
f(x) = x^(1/3), f’(x) = (1/3)x^(−2/3).
Update: x_new = x − f/f’ = x − 3x = −2x.
Starting at 1: 1 → −2 → 4 → −8 → 16 → … It blows up, no convergence.

Gradient Descent:
Minimize 0.5*x^(2/3). Gradient = (1/3)x^(−1/3). Start x0 = 1, η = 0.1.
• x1 ≈ 0.967
• x2 ≈ 0.933
• x3 ≈ 0.899
• x4 ≈ 0.864
• x5 ≈ 0.829
• x6 ≈ 0.794
Slowly but surely moving toward 0.

So here GD works while NR completely diverges.

Overall takeaways

NR is usually much faster if the function is nice and the starting guess is good. But it can completely fail otherwise.

GD is slower, but with a careful step size it’s more stable and reliable.

In practice: NR is great for small, well-behaved problems; GD is what people use for larger or messier cases (like ML).

Topic: Training and testing data , AIC and BIC , Jarque-Bera test , Hyperparameters
YourAnalysis:
In machine learning, the entire point of splitting our data into a training set and a testing set is to check whether the model can truly generalise rather than simply remember. If we train on 100% of the data, there’s no fresh data left to genuinely test the model’s behaviour, which means we risk “fooling ourselves” into thinking it’s performing well. An 80-20 split is commonly used because it offers sufficient data to learn patterns while still preserving a decent chunk for unbiased evaluation. The real insight is that model quality is not only about fitting the past, but being reliable on the future.

AIC and BIC: The Art of Pruning a Model

We can think of AIC and BIC as two very strict editors for a book we're writing. We want our book (our statistical model) to be as accurate as possible, but we also don't want it to be bloated with unnecessary words or chapters (parameters). A model that's too complex might be great at explaining the story we already wrote (the training data) but will utterly fail when trying to tell a new story (unseen data). AIC and BIC are the editors that penalize us for every extra word. A lower value for them means our book is a masterpiece—it tells a compelling story with the fewest words necessary, striking that perfect balance between being informative and concise.

Jarque-Bera Test: A Reality Check on Our Data

Imagine our data is a person, and we're hoping they're perfectly "normal"—symmetrical and well-proportioned. The Jarque-Bera test is like a quick check to see if they fit the profile. It specifically measures if their "skewness" (how lopsided they are) and "kurtosis" (how heavy their tails are) match a normal distribution. When the test gives us a low statistic and a high p-value (greater than 0.05), it's essentially saying, "Hey, I don't see any significant flaws. Our data looks a lot like a normal person, so we can't prove that it isn't." This gives us the green light to proceed with many statistical tests that rely on this assumption, like a doctor giving a clean bill of health.

Hyperparameters: The Car's Control Panel

Think of a machine learning model as a high-performance car. The model's parameters, like the exact position of its pistons and valves, are what the engine learns and optimizes to move forward. But the hyperparameters are the car's control panel, set by the driver before the race even starts. They include crucial settings like the learning rate (how fast the engine revs), the batch size (how much fuel it burns at once), and the number of epochs (how many laps it completes). These settings aren't learned during the drive; they are decided beforehand and fundamentally dictate the car's performance. The process of "hyperparameter tuning" is like a race engineer meticulously adjusting these knobs to squeeze every ounce of performance out of the vehicle and ensure it wins the race.

It assesses whether the sample data's skewness and kurtosis match those of a normal distribution. The Jarque-Bera statistic (JB) is calculated as follows:
JB = n * [S^2/6 + (K-3)^2/24]
Where:
n = number of observations, S = sample skewness, and K = sample kurtosis. 

A higher Jarque-Bera statistic (and a lower p-value) indicates a greater departure from normality.

The Newton-Raphson method is an iterative approach used to solve equations of the type f(x) = 0. It works by starting with an initial approximation and refining it through repeated updates that depend on both the function’s value and its derivative at the current point. Geometrically, this means drawing the tangent line to the curve at the guessed point and finding where that tangent intersects the x-axis; that intersection becomes the next guess.

Because each new step leverages information about both the function and its slope, the method typically converges much faster than simpler approaches.

In optimization settings (such as in machine learning), Newton-Raphson is adapted to find stationary points by solving f′(x) = 0. Here, applying the method to the derivative introduces the involvement of the second derivative, which captures the curvature of the function. This makes the process more accurate for locating minima or maxima compared to basic gradient-based methods.

1. Purpose

Both AIC (Akaike Information Criterion) and BIC (Bayesian Information Criterion) are used for model selection, not for measuring fit like R².
They balance fit (explaining current data) and penalty (avoiding overfitting).
The “better” model is the one with the lower AIC or BIC.

2. Core Difference

AIC:

Based on information theory. Seeks the model that best approximates reality, not necessarily the “true” model.

Penalty = 2k, where k = number of parameters.
Penalty is constant with respect to sample size.

BIC:

Based on Bayesian principles. Seeks the model with the highest probability of being true, assuming the true model is among the candidates.

Penalty = k·ln(n), which increases with sample size (n).

3. Practical Implications

For small datasets (n < 7) → BIC’s penalty (ln(n) < 2) is lighter than AIC’s.

For larger datasets (n ≥ 8) → BIC penalizes more heavily, so it usually prefers simpler models.

AIC tends to allow more complexity, while BIC leans toward parsimony (fewer parameters).

4. Model Comparison Rules

When comparing models:

Lower AIC/BIC is preferred.

Difference Guidelines:

Δ < 2 → Models are essentially equivalent.

2–6 → Some evidence favoring lower value.

6 → Strong evidence favoring lower value.

5. Which to Use?

Use AIC if prediction accuracy is the main goal (e.g., forecasting, machine learning).

Use BIC if explanation and finding the “true” data-generating model matters (e.g., scientific research, theory building).

In practice, both are often computed; if they disagree →

AIC favors complexity, BIC favors simplicity.

Final decision should combine statistics + domain knowledge.

Multiple Linear Regression (MLR) is a statistical technique used to explain the relationship between one dependent variable and several independent variables. Unlike simple regression, which considers only a single predictor, MLR accounts for the fact that most real-world outcomes are influenced by multiple factors simultaneously. The purpose of the model is to measure the strength and direction of each predictor’s influence while holding other predictors constant.

The central principle of MLR is minimizing the difference between actual outcomes and the values predicted by the model. This difference, known as the residual, reflects the error in prediction. The model seeks to minimize the overall error across all observations to ensure the best possible fit. This is achieved by estimating coefficients that represent the contribution of each independent variable to the dependent variable. These coefficients provide a clear interpretation: they show how much the outcome is expected to change with a unit change in the predictor, provided the other variables remain unchanged.

Traditionally, the coefficients of an MLR model can be estimated directly using mathematical equations, but this becomes inefficient and computationally demanding when dealing with large datasets or a high number of predictors. To address this challenge, optimization techniques such as gradient descent are employed.

Gradient descent is an iterative algorithm designed to minimize the error of the model step by step. Instead of calculating the exact solution in one step, it begins with an initial guess of the coefficients and gradually improves them by moving in the direction that reduces the error. Each iteration adjusts the coefficients slightly, based on how much they contribute to the current error. The size of these adjustments is determined by a parameter known as the learning rate. If the learning rate is too high, the process may overshoot and fail to converge; if it is too low, the process may take an impractically long time to reach the optimal values.

One of the main advantages of gradient descent is its scalability. It can handle large amounts of data and high-dimensional problems where direct computation is not feasible. Variations of the algorithm, such as stochastic and mini-batch gradient descent, further enhance efficiency by working with subsets of data at a time rather than the full dataset.

In summary, multiple linear regression provides a structured framework for understanding and quantifying the impact of multiple factors on an outcome, while gradient descent offers a practical and efficient method for estimating the model’s parameters, especially in complex or large-scale scenarios. Together, they form the theoretical and computational backbone of modern predictive analytics and machine learning.

1. Why is it important to interpret coefficients in MLR conditionally rather than absolutely?
In MLR, each coefficient represents the effect of its predictor variable while keeping all other predictors constant. This distinction is crucial because independent variables often overlap in their influence. For example, income and education may both predict job performance, but part of the effect of education is actually channeled through income. If coefficients were interpreted absolutely, we would risk overestimating their impact. By interpreting them conditionally, we isolate the unique contribution of each predictor, even in the presence of correlations among them.

2. What role does multicollinearity play in the validity of MLR results?
Multicollinearity arises when two or more predictors are highly correlated. This does not necessarily harm the predictive power of the model, but it severely complicates interpretation. The model struggles to separate the unique effects of each correlated predictor, leading to unstable coefficients that can vary drastically with small changes in data. From an analytical perspective, this reveals a limitation of MLR: it can tell us that predictors collectively matter, but not always which predictor matters most. Detecting and addressing multicollinearity, through variable selection or dimensionality reduction, is essential for meaningful interpretation.

3. Why is gradient descent preferred over direct computation in certain cases?
Direct computation of regression coefficients is mathematically precise but requires the inversion of large matrices. As the number of predictors or observations grows, this process becomes computationally expensive and sometimes infeasible. Gradient descent avoids this bottleneck by working iteratively. While it does not produce an exact answer immediately, it converges toward the optimal solution with manageable computational effort. This makes it particularly suitable for modern applications involving very large datasets, such as those encountered in machine learning and artificial intelligence.

4. How does the learning rate in gradient descent influence the optimization process?
The learning rate controls the size of the steps taken toward minimizing error. If the learning rate is too high, the algorithm may overshoot the optimal point and fail to converge, oscillating indefinitely. If it is too low, convergence becomes extremely slow and may get stuck in suboptimal positions. Analytically, the learning rate embodies the trade-off between speed and stability. Finding the right value is not just a computational concern but a theoretical one, as it determines whether the algorithm will effectively capture the true underlying relationships.

5. What assumptions underlie the validity of MLR, and why are they significant?
The classical assumptions of MLR include linearity of relationships, independence of errors, homoscedasticity (constant error variance), absence of multicollinearity, and normal distribution of errors. These assumptions are significant because they ensure unbiased and efficient estimation of coefficients. When violated, the model may still produce predictions, but the reliability of interpretation diminishes. For example, if the relationship is not linear, the model systematically underfits; if errors are not independent, the estimated significance of predictors becomes misleading. These assumptions therefore act as the foundation for trustworthy regression analysis.

6. Can MLR and gradient descent guarantee causal inference?
No, neither MLR nor gradient descent can establish causality on their own. MLR quantifies statistical associations, while gradient descent is simply an optimization method that finds the best-fitting coefficients. Without careful research design, including considerations like randomization, instrumental variables, or controlled experiments, regression results remain correlational. This analytical distinction is important because many misinterpret regression outputs as causal evidence, when in fact the method only provides conditional predictions based on observed data.

7. How does the combination of MLR with gradient descent bridge classical statistics and machine learning?
Classical statistics emphasizes theoretical assumptions and exact solutions, while machine learning emphasizes scalability and predictive performance. MLR provides the structured statistical model for understanding relationships, whereas gradient descent provides the computational mechanism to apply this model efficiently to massive datasets. Together, they represent the transition from traditional data analysis to modern machine learning, balancing interpretability with practical feasibility.
