Optimization Criteria in Decision Trees

Decision trees use optimization criteria to decide the “best” split at each node. These criteria measure either how pure the classes become (in classification) or how much prediction error is reduced (in regression).

1. For Classification Trees

The goal is to make child nodes as pure as possible, i.e., containing samples from mainly one class.

Gini Index (used in CART):
Formula: Gini = 1 − Σ (pᵢ)²
Here, pᵢ is the proportion of class i in the node.

A lower Gini means higher purity. If a node has only one class, Gini = 0.

Entropy and Information Gain:
Entropy formula: Entropy = − Σ (pᵢ * log₂ pᵢ)
Information Gain formula: IG = Entropy(parent) − weighted sum of Entropy(children)
Entropy measures “disorder.” A pure node has Entropy = 0. A higher Information Gain means a better split.

Classification Error:
Formula: Error = 1 − max(pᵢ)
It reflects the fraction of incorrectly classified samples if the node were predicted by its majority class. Rarely used in practice because it is less sensitive to changes than Gini or entropy.

2. For Regression Trees

The goal is to minimize prediction error by reducing the variation of target values within each node.

Mean Squared Error (MSE):
Formula: MSE = (1/n) Σ (y − ŷ)²

Sensitive to large errors, so it penalizes outliers heavily.
Splits are chosen to minimize the weighted MSE of child nodes.

Mean Absolute Error (MAE):
Formula: MAE = (1/n) Σ |y − ŷ|

Less sensitive to outliers compared to MSE.
Splits focus on minimizing absolute deviations.

Variance Reduction (used in CART):
Formula: Reduction = Var(parent) − weighted sum of Var(children)

A split is good if it reduces the variance of target values significantly.

Bagging using Random Forest
Decision trees have very low bias and high variance, this leads to increased chance of overfitting. Bagging is a technique which is employed to reduce of the variance by aggregating the results of various low bias and high variance base models. Random Forest applies bagging technique using decision trees as its base model. In this technique the training dataset is sampled randomly and given to each base learning model. This part is called bootstrapping. Now the decision of all the individual models is combined in the aggregation process.

Sampling of Training Data
Suppose we employ m decision tress and feed each of them the entire training dataset, we would have created m clones of a single decision tree. This does not help to reduce the variance. Now  the individual decision trees are provided sampled records from the training dataset with all the features. In this case each record is chosen with replacement from the original dataset, it is called a bootstrap sample. It performs better than the earlier model but each tree will be highly correlated. In order to further reduce the overall variance we sample even the features that is given to the individual trees. This reduces correlation between trees and reduces the overall variance. If the dataset has n features, for classification each tree is given root(n) features and for regression they are given n/3 features to reduce correlation. 

Aggregation
Now that each of the trees are trained on their given data, the final outcome is decided by aggregating the outcomes of individual trees. In case of classification, model outcome is the majority of the individual outcomes. It is called majority vote aggregation. In case of regression the average or median value of the individual outcome is the model's outcome. Mean or median is decided based on the distribution of the individual outcomes. If the distribution of model outcomes is skewed or contains outliers we use median otherwise if it is symmetric and does not contain significant outliers we use mean.

Hyper Parameters
In the case of random forest the hyper parameters are the factors deciding the sampling of features and records, maximum depth and minimum number of observation in leaf of the decision trees. In a bootstrap sample, each record has a 36.8% chance of being left out of a bootstrap sample. Therefore we have a set of testing dataset within the training dataset. We can use them to estimate errors. This is called out of the bag error estimation. Moreover we can also k fold cross validation to tune the hyper parameters.

Metrics
We can use the same metrics used for  linear regression and classification to assess the performance of Random Forest. In case of classification we use precision, recall and f1 score. In case of regression we use RMSE and R2 score.

Limitation
This process is computationally heavy and it does not have a feedback to change the model based on the output error for training data. We must make changes to the model by tuning the hyper parameters. It also picks up noise in the data easily and tries to fit it, resulting in poor performance on testing data. In case of regression it will not be able to predict new values that are out of the range of the given training data, as it is the average of trees whose results are within a range.

Limitations of CART (Classification and Regression Trees)
CART models use a decision tree to split the dataset into regions based on whether the input variables are greater or lesser than some thresholds.
The advantage of CART is that inference is easy: it is easy to explain which features are more important (the ones that appear closer to the root of the decision tree).
However it suffers from the inference-predictive power tradeoff: it makes too simple assumptions about the underlying model, and so suffers in test accuracy.
1. For example, splitting regions based on thresholds results in hard boundaries, instead of smooth probabilistic variation in its decision.
2. Any one node of the decision tree checks the value of only one input variable. During regression, this results in the predicted lines being parallel to the feature axes, with sharp corners where the lines meet. It struggles to predict continuous functions. This is something linear models are especially good at.
3. Finally CART suffers from overfitting: as the depth of the tree increases, CART makes special cases for individual outlier points, resulting in spikes when splitting the dataset.
In practice it is found that the particular tree structure that is learned by CART is very sensitive to the details of the data set, so that a small change to the training data can result in a very different set of splits.


Consider the problem of how to determine the structure of the decision tree. Checking all possible trees is computationally infeasible due to the combinatorially large number of possible solutions. Instead, a greedy opti-
mization is done by starting with the root node, corresponding to the whole input space, and then growing the tree by adding nodes one at a time. At each step, the threshold is chosen such that the error at that step is minimized. This greedy strategy misses trees where a weak decision earlier on is followed by a much better decision later.
To decide when to stop growing the tree, a large tree is grown, stop based on the number of samples per leaf, and then prune back the resulting tree. The pruning is based on a criterion that balances error vs the model's complexity.
For regression, simply a regularization parameter lambda is used, and a term lambda*leaf_count is added to the error.
For classification problems, the process of growing and pruning the tree is similar, except that the sum-of-squares error is replaced by a more appropriate measure of performance. Two commonly used choices are the Gini index and the cross-entropy. If p is the fraction of data points in a region assigned to class k, the Gini index is a summation over k of p*(1-p), while the cross entropy is a summation of p*log(p).
Both these measures vanish at p=0 and 1, and are maximum at p=0.5.
They increase the formation of regions in which a high proportion of the data points are
assigned to one class. I.e., they reduce mixing of classes. The cross entropy and the Gini index are better measures than the misclassification rate for growing the tree because they are more sensitive to the node probabilities. Also, unlike the misclassification rate, they are differentiable functions and so better suited to gradient based optimization.


Bagging and boosting are variants of the committee method, which averages the predictions made by a combination of models called a committee. Their utility derives from the fundamental statistical principle that the average error from a set of samples, is 1/M times the error of one sample, where M is the number of samples. If the errors of the different models of the committee are uncorrelated, we can increase accuracy simply by increasing the number of models. In practice, the errors are typically highly correlated, and the reduction in overall error is generally small. However, it can be shown that the expected committee error will not exceed the expected error of the constituent models.


Mixture-of-Experts (MoE)
We can extend the flexibility of mixing models by allowing the mixing coefficients to themselves be functions of the input variables. This is known as a mixture of experts model, where both the models (called experts) and the weights (called gating functions) are learned. Each expert models the distribution in different regions of input space differently.
MoE has found great applications in deep learning as a simple way to perform conditional computation: only parts of the model are used, the parts chosen according to what the input is. This greatly improves the efficiency of the model. This was a major reason behind the success of the Deepseek transformer architecture. Researchers at DeepSeek designed a variant of MoE, with "shared experts" that are always queried, and "routed experts" that might not be. They found that usual optimization causes experts to replicate the same core skills, such as English grammar. They proposed the shared experts to learn core capacities that are often used, and let the routed experts to learn the peripheral capacities that are rarely used.
This shows the power of techniques which aggregate over multiple models.

Topic: Optimization criteria used in Decision Tree - for regression and classification
YourAnalysis:
Introduction
Decision Trees are powerful because they are simple to interpret yet capable of modeling complex decision boundaries. However, their behavior is not “automatic” — it is deeply shaped by the optimization criterion used for splitting nodes. 
In this analysis, I focus not only on describing the criteria (Gini, entropy, MSE, etc.) but also reflecting on why they exist, what trade-offs they imply, and how their choice influences real-world outcomes.
Central Idea
At each node, the tree asks: “Which split best separates the data?” 
- For classification, this means reducing uncertainty about the class labels. 
- For regression, this means reducing prediction error for continuous outcomes. 

What is striking is that trees are greedy: they decide based only on immediate purity/error reduction, not on long-term outcomes. This makes the split criterion even more critical because it drives every step of the tree’s construction.
Classification Criteria
1. Gini Impurity 
   - Formula: Gini = 1 − Σ(pᵢ²).  
   - Intuition: High Gini means the node is “mixed.” A good split lowers Gini, pushing nodes toward class homogeneity.  
   - Comment: I find Gini computationally elegant — just squaring proportions — and its convex nature rewards splits that reduce heterogeneity.  

2. Entropy (Information Gain)  
   - Formula: Entropy = −Σ(pᵢ log₂ pᵢ).  
   - Intuition: Derived from information theory, it measures “disorder.” Information gain quantifies how much uncertainty a split removes.  
   - Comment: Entropy appeals philosophically: it connects decision trees with Shannon’s theory of information. However, in practice, its splits often resemble Gini’s.  

3. Misclassification Error  
   - Formula: Error = 1 − max(pᵢ).  
   - Intuition: Only cares about the majority class proportion.  
   - Comment: While conceptually simple, it is less sensitive to class distribution changes, so I see why it is rarely used in tree growth (though useful for pruning).
Regression Criteria
1. Mean Squared Error (MSE)
   - Formula: MSE = (1/n) Σ (y − ŷ)².  
   - Comment: MSE penalizes large deviations heavily. This makes regression trees “chase” outliers, sometimes splitting excessively to minimize squared errors.  

2. Mean Absolute Error (MAE)
   - Formula: MAE = (1/n) Σ |y − ŷ|.  
   - Comment: MAE is more robust to outliers. But because it is less smooth mathematically, it is harder to optimize greedily.  

Analytically, both measures define what “purity” means for regression: how tightly values cluster. The trade-off is essentially: sensitivity to extremes (MSE) versus robustness (MAE).
Why the Criterion Choice Matters
The optimization criterion influences:
- Tree structure: A split chosen under entropy might differ slightly from one under Gini. These differences cascade, shaping the overall tree.  
- Interpretability: Simpler splits sometimes emerge from criteria that are less “fussy” about tiny distribution changes.  
- Bias-variance trade-off: A criterion too sensitive to minor changes (like MSE with outliers) can lead to deeper, more variable trees.  

In essence, the criterion encodes the tree’s definition of “goodness.” I realized this makes them less arbitrary and more philosophical — they formalize *what we value* in prediction: certainty, error minimization, or robustness.
Limitations and Risks
- Greedy approach: Trees optimize splits locally, which might not produce globally optimal partitions.  
- Overfitting: Sensitive criteria can generate trees that capture noise.  
- Small data instability: Slight changes in data may lead to very different splits, especially under entropy or MSE.  

These limitations highlight why pruning or ensembles (forests, boosting) are usually essential. The split criterion alone cannot “guard” against overfitting.
Broader Context and Extensions
- Random Forests: Average across many trees, reducing sensitivity to one criterion’s quirks.  
- Boosted Trees: Optimize flexible loss functions (logistic, Huber, etc.) beyond just Gini or MSE.  
- Cost-sensitive learning: Especially in medical settings, false positives and negatives may not be symmetric, motivating tailored split objectives.  

Thus, decision trees are part of a larger ecosystem of methods — but their optimization criteria remain the foundational “atoms” of this ecosystem.
Conclusion
- Classification trees rely on Gini, entropy, or error reduction; regression trees rely on variance minimization via MSE/MAE.  
- The choice of criterion subtly affects splits, interpretability, and sensitivity to outliers.  
- While simple to state, these criteria are central: they define how the tree “thinks.”  
- Best practice: use Gini/Entropy for classification, MSE for regression, but always pair with pruning/ensembles to mitigate risks.  

Ultimately, optimization criteria are not trivial details but the hidden levers shaping decision trees. This analysis convinced me that understanding them is essential to using trees thoughtfully.

Decision Trees are high-variance models. This means that a small change in input data produces a huge variation in the output and therefore can produce a completely different tree. Optimization criteria in decision trees are the rules used to decide how to split the data at each node to best separate or predict the target variable. These criteria differ depending on whether the tree is used for classification or regression tasks.

For Classification:
The goal is to find splits that produce "pure" nodes, where most samples belong to a single class. The commonly used criteria are:
Gini Impurity: Measures the probability that a randomly chosen sample would be mislabeled if it were randomly labeled according to the distribution of classes in the node. Lower values indicate better splits.
First for each class within a node calculate the probability of that class This is done by dividing the number of samples of that class by the total number of samples in the node
Second square the probability of each class
Third sum all the squared probabilities together
Fourth subtract this sum from the number one The result is the Gini impurity
So the Gini impurity for this particular node is zero point four two
Entropy (Information Gain): Measures the amount of uncertainty or disorder in the node. The split with the highest information gain (reduction in entropy) is chosen.
These criteria guide the tree to create splits that group samples of the same class together, improving classification accuracy.
For Regression:
The target is numerical, so the tree aims to find splits that minimize the variance or error within each node. Typical criteria include:
Mean Squared Error (MSE): It measures the average squared difference between actual and predicted values in a node. The split that results in the largest reduction in MSE is chosen.
Other criteria like Mean Absolute Error (MAE) or Poisson Deviance can also be used.
The predicted value for each leaf node is usually the average of the target values of samples within that node.
In both cases, the optimization criteria are used recursively to decide the best feature and threshold to split nodes until stopping conditions (like maximum depth or minimum samples per leaf) are met. This process constructs the tree by partitioning the data space into regions that are as homogeneous as possible regarding the target variable.

Topic: BAGGING as implemented in Random Forest
YourAnalysis:
Bagging, short for Bootstrap Aggregating, is an ensemble method designed to reduce variance and improve the stability of machine learning models. The idea is simple: instead of relying on a single predictive model, bagging trains multiple models on different subsets of the training data and then combines their predictions.

Random Forests extend bagging by introducing additional randomness in feature selection, making them one of the most powerful and widely used tree-based ensemble methods.

It starts with the original dataset of size N, Random Forest draws B bootstrap samples (each of size N but sampled with replacement). Each decision tree is trained on one of these bootstrap samples. On average, around 63% of unique samples appear in each bootstrap set; the remaining ~37% form the out-of-bag (OOB) set for that tree.

Each bootstrap dataset trains a decision tree. Unlike a standard CART, Random Forests add randomness by selecting a random subset of features at each split, preventing trees from becoming too correlated. For Classification: Random Forest takes a majority vote across all trees. For Regression: Random Forest averages the outputs of all trees.

The reason bagging works in random forests is because individual decision trees are high-variance models (slight changes in data can lead to different splits). By aggregating predictions from many independently trained trees, Random Forest reduces variance drastically. Since each tree is trained on a slightly different dataset and different feature subsets, the ensemble is less sensitive to noise and outliers compared to a single decision tree.

Since each tree is trained without some portion (~37%) of data, these unseen samples can be used to test that tree. Aggregating across all trees, OOB provides an unbiased estimate of model performance without requiring a separate validation set. This makes Random Forests computationally efficient and self-validating. 

The advantages of bagging include improved generalization as aggregation leads to smoother decision boundaries and avoids overfitting. Individual outliers have little effect since they are averaged out across many trees. Bagging is easily parallelizable, as each tree is trained independently. Lastly, due to feature randomness, Random Forests can naturally rank features by importance, which is useful for interpretation.

To conclude, bagging in Random Forests is the critical piece that stabilizes decision trees, reduces variance, and boosts predictive accuracy. By combining bootstrap sampling, feature randomness, and aggregation, Random Forests create a balanced, high-performing model that generalizes well to unseen data.

Boosting methods build trees sequentially, with each new tree correcting errors from the previous ones.

Within boosting, XGBoost is popular for its efficiency and regularization, LightGBM for its speed and ability to handle large datasets, and CatBoost for directly managing categorical features.

These algorithms are popular because they preserve the flexibility of decision trees while improving accuracy, scalability, and robustness, making them highly effective for real-world machine learning tasks.

Random forests are perhaps the most widely used machine learning method in the world today, and rightly so. Fundamentally, they consist of decision trees—simple models that bifurcate data into branches until they arrive at a decision. The weakness with individual trees, though, is that they are brittle. A slight perturbation in the data can totally alter the shape of the tree, and hence its decisions. Random forests overcome this by taking lots of trees and training them slightly differently. All their predictions averaged together give a much more stable and trustworthy result.
The largest advantage of random forests is that they are extremely good at minimizing variance. In the real world, what this translates to is that they are less likely to provide drastically different responses when presented with new data. For instance, in dirty real-world problems such as predicting customers' behavior or disease diagnosis, getting a solid, reliable prediction is sometimes more valuable than an optimal one. Random forests also excel when handling high-dimensional data—datasets with hundreds or thousands of features—because they naturally pay more attention to the relevant features and pay little attention to most of the noise.
But these advantages do have some significant trade-offs. A single decision tree is simple to understand—you can trace the branches like a flowchart and clearly understand why a prediction was made. Random forests are far more difficult to interpret, however. When hundreds of trees are combined in an ensemble, the reasoning behind a specific prediction is virtually impossible to follow directly. In domains where explanations are important, such as law or medicine, this "black box" quality is a significant disadvantage.
Another drawback is that random forests are not able to extrapolate outside the range they have witnessed. They operate by bisecting data into segments and making static predictions in those segments. If required to predict below the training interval—for example, what could transpire in some emerging trend they have never witnessed—they fail. More basic models such as linear regression, although less precise as a whole, can at times deal with the situation more competently.
There are also practical considerations. There is a lot of computation and memory required to train a forest of big trees and hence they are slower than alternatives. New boosting algorithms such as XGBoost are therefore generally the choice in industry since they have similar or better accuracy with less resource consumption. And while random forests can give estimates of "feature importance," these numbers can be deceptive, overestimating the contributions of some variables at times.
So, when do we use random forests? They are especially useful when the need is precise prediction on noisy, high-dimensional data and when we don't need an explicit explanation for all the results. They are not ideal when transparency is crucial or if the task is more complicated and predictions need to be made outside the data we have.
In summary, random forests are formidable tools that strike a balance between complexity and stability. They excel at variance reduction and noise handling, yet they do not lack flaws. Similar to most techniques in machine learning, their value relies not only on their sheer brute force, but also on whether or not their trade-offs align with the problem in question.

# Comparative Analysis of CART, Bagging/Random Forest, and Boosting (GBDT)

CART (Classification and Regression Trees), Bagging/Random Forest, and Boosting/GBDT are foundational ensemble machine learning algorithms, each with distinctive strengths and limitations. This analysis goes beyond textbook characteristics to explore the nuanced mechanisms and trade-offs that shape their role in real-world modeling.

---

## CART: Interpretability Versus Flexibility

CART is a single decision tree algorithm that recursively splits data based on feature thresholds, creating a hierarchical set of decision rules. The principal advantage of **CART** is its exceptional interpretability, models can be visualized as flowcharts, making it straightforward to trace how input features influence output predictions. Business users and domain experts value such transparency, especially for regulatory and operational decision-making.

CART’s simplicity, however, is a double-edged sword. While it can naturally model non-linear relationships and handle mixed data types, its predictions are highly unstable. A slight perturbation in training data can lead to drastically different splits and thus very different trees. This instability makes CART unreliable in high-stakes domains unless supported by ensemble methods.

The other major limitation is **overfitting**. Deep trees tend to memorize training data quirks, producing excellent training accuracy but weak generalization. Pruning helps, yet the pruning decision itself is non-trivial: prune too aggressively, and bias dominates; prune too lightly, and variance overwhelms. Moreover, because splits are greedy (locally optimal), CART can miss **global feature interactions**, subtle effects that only emerge when multiple features act in concert. For example, two features may individually appear weak, but together strongly separate classes; CART may overlook this unless the right splits occur early.

Thus, CART is best understood not as a final predictive model but as a **building block**: useful for interpretability, feature exploration, and rapid prototyping, but limited in robustness when used alone.

---

## Bagging and Random Forest: Reducing Variance and Enhancing Stability

Bagging (Bootstrap Aggregation) addresses CART’s instability by averaging across many trees trained on bootstrapped samples of the data. **Random Forest** improves upon Bagging by injecting feature-level randomness at each split, reducing correlation among trees and further lowering variance.

The most significant advantage here is **robustness**. By aggregating diverse trees, Random Forest smooths out noise, reduces variance, and produces more stable predictions. It works well on datasets with heterogeneous feature types, is tolerant of outliers, and provides measures of feature importance, making it a versatile general-purpose tool.

However, these benefits come with trade-offs:

- **Computational cost**: Training and evaluating hundreds or thousands of trees is resource-intensive. For large datasets or latency-sensitive applications (e.g., fraud detection in live transactions), this can be a bottleneck.
    
- **Interpretability**: While global measures like feature importance or SHAP values can be extracted, the ensemble’s decision process is opaque. A single tree is human-readable; a forest of 1,000 trees is not. This lack of transparency can pose challenges in regulated domains such as healthcare or finance.
    
- **Residual overfitting risk**: Although variance is reduced, Random Forests can still overfit, especially on small datasets or if trees are grown excessively deep. The randomness mitigates correlation but does not eliminate the risk of memorizing noise.
    

In practice, Random Forest often strikes an appealing balance: it requires less hyperparameter tuning than Boosting and generally performs well “out of the box.” It is especially suited to domains where stability and robustness outweigh the absolute push for maximum accuracy.

---

## Boosting/GBDT: Harnessing Weak Learners and Sensitivity to Data

Boosting takes the opposite approach to Bagging: instead of training trees independently and aggregating, it trains them **sequentially**, with each new tree correcting the errors of the previous ensemble. Gradient Boosted Decision Trees (GBDT) implement this by fitting trees to the negative gradient of the loss function, iteratively reducing residuals.

This mechanism gives Boosting its **power**. By concentrating effort on hard-to-predict cases, GBDT achieves lower bias and often higher predictive accuracy than Random Forest. It is especially effective in structured/tabular data where relationships are subtle and nonlinear. Indeed, many machine learning competitions are won with variants of GBDT (e.g., XGBoost, LightGBM, CatBoost).

But Boosting’s strength is inseparable from its **fragility**:

- **Overfitting risk**: If boosting is run too long or trees are too deep, the model memorizes noise. Regularization techniques (shrinkage/learning rate, subsampling, early stopping) are essential.
    
- **Sensitivity to data**: Boosting can amplify noise and bias towards majority classes unless mitigated with weighting schemes or sampling. In sparse, high-dimensional data, it may chase spurious patterns rather than meaningful ones.
    
- **Computational demands**: Unlike Random Forest, trees in Boosting cannot be trained in parallel because each depends on the errors of the previous. This sequential nature makes training slower, though modern optimized libraries have narrowed this gap.
    
- **Interpretability**: Even more than Random Forest, Boosting sacrifices transparency for accuracy. Post-hoc interpretability tools are required to make its decisions explainable.
    

In short, Boosting delivers **peak predictive accuracy** when carefully tuned, but requires expertise, computational resources, and strong validation pipelines to avoid overfitting.

---

## Practical Trade-offs and Use Cases

The choice among CART, Random Forest, and Boosting is not simply one of “better versus worse,” but of **trade-offs aligned to context**:

- **CART**: Useful for interpretable decision-making, feature exploration, and rule-based systems. A good first model but rarely the final one.
    
- **Random Forest**: Strong baseline for structured data, robust under noise, minimal tuning required. Well-suited to operational systems where interpretability is not the highest priority but stability is.
    
- **Boosting/GBDT**: Ideal for competition-level accuracy, ranking problems (search engines, recommender systems), and scenarios where incremental accuracy gains translate into significant business value. Demands careful tuning and regularization.
    

Thus, the practical choice depends less on raw accuracy and more on the **interaction between interpretability, stability, computation, and domain requirements**.

---

## Summary Table

|Algorithm|Key Strengths|Key Limitations|
|---|---|---|
|CART|**Interpretable**, easy visualization|Unstable, overfits easily, misses global interactions|
|Random Forest|**Reduces variance**, robust, handles varied data|Resource-heavy, opaque, residual overfitting risk|
|Boosting/GBDT|**Maximizes accuracy**, minimizes bias, strong learner|Prone to overfitting, slower, sensitive to data noise|

---

## Conclusion

CART, Bagging/Random Forest, and Boosting are not competitors so much as **complementary tools**. CART offers transparency but limited reliability; Random Forest provides robustness with moderate complexity; Boosting delivers accuracy at the cost of sensitivity and computational burden. A practitioner’s skill lies in recognizing which trade-offs matter most for their domain, whether it is the clarity demanded in healthcare, the robustness needed in fraud detection, or the competitive edge required in data science contests.

In decision trees, the optimization criteria determine how splits are chosen at each node. The goal is to maximize the “purity” of child nodes by minimizing some measure of impurity or error.

For classification, common criteria are based on class impurity. The most widely used are Gini index and entropy (information gain). The Gini index measures the probability of incorrect classification if a label is chosen randomly from a node, while entropy quantifies the information needed to represent the class distribution. A split is chosen to minimize these impurity measures, resulting in child nodes that are as homogeneous as possible. Some implementations also use classification error rate, though it is less sensitive and therefore less common.

For regression, the focus shifts to predicting continuous outputs, so impurity is measured by deviation from the mean. The most common criterion is variance reduction, often operationalized as minimizing the mean squared error (MSE) within nodes. Alternatives include mean absolute error (MAE) and reductions in standard deviation. In all cases, the split is selected to produce child nodes where target values are as concentrated as possible around their means.

Thus, classification trees optimize for class purity, while regression trees optimize for variance reduction, both seeking splits that yield more informative and predictive partitions of the data.

Classification and Regression Trees (CART)
A Decision Tree is a predictive model that uses a flowchart-like structure to arrive at a conclusion. It works by asking a series of sequential questions about the data, where each question splits the data into smaller, more homogenous groups. The CART algorithm is a specific method used to generate these trees for two types of tasks:
Classification: Used when the goal is to predict a categorical label (e.g., 'spam' or 'not spam', 'approve' or 'deny'). The tree sorts data into predefined classes.
Regression: Used when the goal is to predict a continuous numerical value (e.g., the price of a house, the temperature tomorrow). The tree estimates a numeric outcome.
The final prediction is found at a "leaf node" at the end of a path of questions.

Limitations of CART Decision Trees
Single decision trees are powerful but have several key limitations.

1)Overfitting: Trees are prone to becoming overly complex by learning the noise and specific details of the training data. This causes the model to perform poorly when it encounters new, unseen data because it has not learned the general underlying pattern.

2)Instability (High Variance): The structure of a decision tree can change drastically with small variations in the training data. Removing or adding a few data points can result in a completely different tree, making the model feel unreliable and not robust.

3)Inability to Model Linear Relationships: A tree makes splits that are parallel to the data axes (e.g., feature_A > 10). This creates rectangular decision boundaries. If the true relationship between features is linear or diagonal, the tree must approximate it with a clumsy "staircase" of many small splits, making the model inefficient and overly complex.

4)Bias Toward Features with More Categories: When a dataset contains categorical features, the algorithm may be unfairly biased towards features with a large number of levels (e.g., a 'City' column with 50 options). It may select this feature for a split over a more predictive feature simply because the numerous categories offer more ways to divide the data.

Bagging
Bagging (Bootstrap Aggregating) is an ensemble technique designed to reduce the instability (variance) of a single decision tree. It leverages the "wisdom of the crowd" by combining the outputs of many models.

The process is as follows:

Multiple random subsets of the original training data are created using a technique called bootstrapping (sampling with replacement).

A separate decision tree is trained independently on each of these data subsets. This creates a collection of diverse trees, often called a "forest."

For a new prediction, the results from all trees are aggregated. In classification, this is done by majority vote; in regression, the predictions are averaged.

A prominent example of bagging is the Random Forest algorithm, which is known for its high accuracy and resistance to overfitting.

Boosting
Boosting is another ensemble technique, but it builds models sequentially, where each new model is trained to correct the errors of the previous ones. The goal is to combine many "weak learners" (simple models) into a single "strong learner."

The process is as follows:
A simple decision tree is trained on the data.
The algorithm identifies the data points that the tree misclassified. These incorrect predictions are given more weight or importance.
A second tree is trained, which pays more attention to the high-weight (previously incorrect) data points.
This process is repeated many times, with each successive model focusing on the mistakes that the entire ensemble is still making.
The final prediction is a weighted combination of all the models' outputs. Boosting algorithms like Gradient Boosting and XGBoost are often among the top performers in machine learning competitions due to their high predictive accuracy.

A decision tree is a machine learning model that looks like a flowchart and is used for making predictions or decisions. It is called a "tree" because it starts with a single point at the top, known as the root, and then branches out into smaller decision points, eventually ending in leaves that represent the final outcomes.

When a decision tree is built, its core task is to decide where to split the data at each step. The quality of a split is judged using something called an optimization criterion. In simple words, this criterion tells the tree: “Is this split making the groups purer or more organized?” For classification problems, purity means that each group contains mostly one class, while for regression problems, it means the values in each group are close together with little variation.

In classification trees, two main criteria are used: Gini index and entropy. Both of these measure how mixed the classes are within a node. If a node contains data from only one class, it is said to be perfectly pure, and the impurity measures take a value of zero. The Gini index is defined as 
1-sigma​(pi)^2	
where pi is the proportion of class i

If the classes are evenly mixed (say, 50% A and 50% B), the Gini index reaches higher values, signaling more impurity. Entropy works in a similar way but comes from information theory. It is defined as 
-sigma pi*log2(pi)

it measures the uncertainty in the node. A node with equal proportions of different classes has maximum entropy, while a pure node has entropy zero. In practice, the tree compares possible splits and chooses the one that reduces impurity (or increases information gain) the most.

For regression trees, the story is a little different. Instead of worrying about class purity, the goal is to make groups where the numerical values are as similar as possible. 
The most common criterion here is Mean Squared Error (MSE), which measures how far the values in a node are from their average. A node where values are tightly clustered around the mean has a small MSE, which indicates a good split. Another option is Mean Absolute Error (MAE), which instead of squaring the deviations just takes their absolute value, making it less sensitive to outliers. Again, the decision tree evaluates possible splits and prefers the one that minimizes error in the child nodes.

The reason these formulas work is that they directly capture what we want the tree to achieve: in classification, we want each branch to separate the classes as cleanly as possible; in regression, we want each branch to make predictions that are as accurate as possible. By reducing impurity or minimizing error step by step, the tree gradually organizes the data into meaningful partitions.

In layman's terms, building a decision tree is like sorting marbles into jars. If we are sorting by color (a classification task), a good split means that each jar contains marbles of mostly one color. If we are sorting by size (a regression task), a good split means that each jar contains marbles of roughly the same size. The optimization criteria are simply the rules the tree uses to decide which split is “better” as it goes about organizing the marbles.

Decision trees are hierarchical models that partition data recursively. The key issue in building a tree is deciding where to split at each level, as the quality of a tree is directly related to the efficacy of splits. Each split is tested against an optimization criterion, which measures how much better the resulting partitions are than the parent node.

In classification, we want to maximize class homogeneity in our nodes; the Gini index and entropy are two often-used impurity indicators. With both indicators, there is a measurement of the amount of class mix, but their design is not the same; Gini uses the squared probabilities of the classes, while entropy is concerned with information theory uncertainty and logs.  The most optimal split should minimize the impurity in the child nodes compared to the parent node, regardless of the indicator used to gauge impurity.

In regression, rather than focusing on purity, we focus on reducing variance. For this purpose, we can use criteria such as the Mean Squared Error (MSE) and the Mean Absolute Error (MAE) to measure variability within a node. If we can minimize these, it indicates that the partition buckets groups the observations using a central tendency that is fixed, which should help improve the accuracy of the predictions.

Each time the model makes a split, it chooses a locally optimal cut, and there is no concern for future splits. This will speed up the calculations but also illustrates why trees are challenging without some form of pruning or ensemble approach because they can quickly learn a model that has little to do with reality, hence, overfitted.

So, we can think of the decision tree as no longer being a type of flow chart used to sort, and instead we can think of it as a recursive optimization process, where every step maximizes information gain (for classification) or minimizes prediction error (for regression), by recursively organizing the data into partitions which deliver some approximation of the underlying decision boundaries.

Decision trees are supervised learning models that split data into branches based on feature values. The way these splits are chosen depends on an optimization criterion, which ensures that each division creates the most informative separation possible. The criteria differ depending on whether the tree is used for classification or regression.

For classification trees, where the target variable is categorical, the goal of the optimization criterion is to maximize class purity in the resulting subsets. The most commonly used measures are Gini impurity and entropy. Gini impurity measures how often a randomly chosen element would be incorrectly labeled if it were randomly assigned a label according to the distribution in the node. Lower Gini values indicate purer nodes, and CART (Classification and Regression Trees) typically uses this measure. Entropy, used in algorithms like ID3 and C4.5, comes from information theory and quantifies the uncertainty in a node. A split is considered better if it reduces entropy, which is measured as information gain. Another possible criterion is misclassification error, which simply looks at the proportion of misclassified examples, though it is less sensitive and mainly used in pruning stages rather than for initial splits.

For regression trees, where the target variable is continuous, the optimization criterion focuses on reducing prediction error. The most widely used measure is the mean squared error (MSE), which evaluates how much the predicted values at each node deviate from the actual outputs. A split is chosen if it significantly reduces the overall variance within the child nodes compared to the parent node. Another option is mean absolute error (MAE), which uses the median as the representative prediction instead of the mean, making it more robust to outliers. However, MSE is more commonly used because it is mathematically easier to optimize.

In summary, decision trees rely on different optimization criteria depending on the problem type. For classification, purity measures such as Gini impurity and entropy are used to ensure that the classes are as homogeneous as possible after each split. For regression, error measures such as mean squared error or mean absolute error are used to ensure that predictions are close to the actual numerical values. The choice of criterion influences the final structure of the tree and its performance, but in practice, most implementations default to Gini for classification and MSE for regression.

Low Predictive Accuracy Compared to Ensembles – While interpretable, standalone CART models are often weaker than ensemble methods such as Random Forest or Boosting.

Instability in Deeper Trees – Trees can become large and complex, leading to reduced generalization ability.

Advantages:

Reduces Variance – By aggregating predictions from multiple CART models trained on bootstrapped samples, Random Forest reduces the instability of a single tree.

Improved Accuracy – Generally provides better predictive performance than standalone decision trees due to averaging across multiple models.

Handles High-Dimensional Data – Can work efficiently even with large numbers of features and samples.

Feature Importance – Provides measures of feature importance (via Gini importance or permutation importance), which help in interpretability and feature selection.

Robustness – Less sensitive to outliers, noise, and overfitting compared to individual trees.

Parallelizable – Each tree can be trained independently, making Random Forest suitable for distributed and parallel computation.

Reduced Interpretability – While individual trees are interpretable, the ensemble of hundreds of trees acts more like a “black box.”

Less Effective for Extrapolation in Regression – Random Forest predictions are averages of trees, so they may struggle to predict values outside the range of the training data.

Not Always Best for Sparse/High-Correlation Data – When features are highly correlated, Random Forest can suffer from redundancy, reducing efficiency.

3) Boosting (Gradient Boosted Decision Trees – GBDT)

Advantages:

High Predictive Power – Boosting often achieves state-of-the-art accuracy in classification and regression problems. GBDT models frequently outperform bagging-based methods like Random Forest.

Bias Reduction – Sequentially corrects the errors of previous learners, reducing bias and building strong learners from weak ones.

Handles Complex Data Patterns – Effective at capturing intricate feature interactions and nonlinear relationships.

Flexibility – Can optimize various loss functions (e.g., logistic, exponential, squared error), making it applicable to classification, regression, and ranking tasks.

Overfitting Risk – If not properly regularized (learning rate, tree depth, number of iterations), boosting can overfit to noise in the data.

Topic: Optimization criteria used in Decision Tree - for regression and classification
YourAnalysis:
Decision trees are a cornerstone of machine learning models, widely used for both classification and regression tasks due to their interpretability, computational efficiency and ability to handle both categorical and numerical data. The performance of a decision tree critically depends on how it decides to split the data at each node. This decision is driven by optimization criteria—quantitative measures used to evaluate the “quality” of a potential split. These criteria differ for classification and regression, as the nature of the prediction task dictates the notion of “purity” or “homogeneity” in the resulting child nodes.
For classification problems, the goal is to partition the data such that each resulting subset is as homogeneous as possible with respect to the target class labels. Three primary metrics are widely used: Gini Impurity, Information Gain (based on entropy),and classification error.
Gini Impurity measures the probability of incorrectly classifying a randomly chosen element if it were labeled according to the distribution of classes in that subset. It is defined as the sum over all classes of the probability of a class multiplied by one minus that probability. A perfectly pure node (all samples belong to a single class) has a Gini Impurity of zero, whereas a completely mixed node has a higher impurity. Decision tree algorithms such as CART (Classification and Regression Trees) commonly use Gini Impurity because it is computationally efficient and tends to produce well-balanced trees.
Information Gain relies on entropy, a measure from information theory quantifying the amount of uncertainty or disorder in a dataset. A node with high entropy has a roughly uniform distribution of classes, while low entropy indicates that the classes are concentrated in fewer categories. When a split reduces entropy significantly, it increases information gain, meaning that the split provides substantial clarity about class membership. This metric is central to algorithms such as ID3 and C4.5, which prioritize splits that maximize information gain. A less common but conceptually straightforward criterion is classification error, which measures the fraction of samples not belonging to the majority class in a node. While simple, it is less sensitive than Gini or entropy and thus less commonly used.
For regression problems, the optimization criteria shift focus from class purity to prediction accuracy regarding a continuous target variable. The core principle is to minimize the variance of the target values within each node, producing partitions where the values are as similar as possible. Two widely used metrics are variance reduction and mean squared error (MSE).
Variance reduction evaluates how much splitting a node decreases the variability of target values in the resulting child nodes. A good split significantly lowers variance, meaning that samples within each branch are more tightly clustered around their respective means. MSE, closely related, computes the average squared deviation of target values from their mean within a node. Minimizing MSE aligns directly with minimizing the expected squared error of predictions. In essence, the model learns partitions where the mean target value serves as a strong predictor for all instances in that leaf.
The choice of optimization criterion affects tree structure, interpretability, and ultimately model performance. Gini and entropy often produce similar trees, though subtle differences can matter in imbalanced datasets. Variance reduction and MSE-based criteria emphasize regions where prediction uncertainty is minimized, which is critical for robust regression performance. Additionally, the depth of the tree, pruning strategies, and sample weights interact with these criteria, influencing overfitting, bias, and variance trade-offs.
Understanding these optimization criteria is not merely a technical detail—it directly informs decisions in model selection, hyperparameter tuning, and even feature engineering. By aligning the criterion with the characteristics of the data and the problem, practitioners can balance accuracy, complexity, and interpretability, ultimately leveraging decision trees as precise, data-driven instruments for predictive analytics.

Decision trees use different optimization criteria depending on the task. For classification, they typically use measures like Gini impurity or entropy to decide the best splits that create homogeneous class groups. For regression, they minimize variance or mean squared error within the nodes to achieve accurate continuous value predictions.

Bagging, as implemented in Random Forest, involves creating multiple decision trees on different random subsets of the training data and averaging their predictions (for regression) or taking a majority vote (for classification). This approach reduces variance and helps prevent overfitting compared to a single decision tree.

Boosting, as implemented in Gradient Boosting Decision Trees (GBDT), builds trees sequentially, where each new tree focuses on correcting the errors of the previous ones by optimizing a loss function through gradient descent. This process reduces bias and can achieve high predictive accuracy but is more prone to overfitting if not carefully regularized.

Each of these algorithms has distinct advantages and limitations. CART (Classification and Regression Trees) is simple and interpretable but can overfit without pruning. Bagging with Random Forest improves stability and accuracy, handling large feature spaces well but at the cost of less interpretability. Boosting through GBDT offers powerful prediction ability but requires careful tuning and longer training time.

Other popular decision tree-based algorithms include XGBoost and LightGBM, known for their speed and efficiency in large-scale problems.

CART (Classification and Regression Trees) are widely used for classification and regression because they are simple, interpretable, and flexible. But they also have clear weaknesses:

They struggle with certain kinds of observations and relationships.

2. Mathematical Approach

CART splits data recursively using rules like:

For classification:

Choose split that maximizes information gain / reduces Gini impurity.

For regression:

Choose split that minimizes variance (mean squared error).

Situations where this fails:

High Variance / Overfitting

CART tries to perfectly separate training data.

As depth grows, training error → 0, but test error ↑ (overfitting).

Unstable Splits

Small changes in data can completely change the top-level split.

This instability is because each split is greedy (local optimum), not globally optimal.

Poor with Linear / Smooth Boundaries

CART makes axis-aligned splits (vertical/horizontal cuts).

If the true relationship is diagonal or curved (e.g., y = x line), CART struggles unless the tree is very deep.

Bias in Imbalanced Data

If one class dominates, CART can favor it because splits may not reduce impurity enough for minority classes.

Noisy Data / Outliers

Outliers can affect splits heavily → poor generalization.

Small Sample Sizes

With very few samples per leaf, variance is high, predictions unreliable.

Continuous Variables with Many Close Values

CART may keep splitting unnecessarily on small differences, failing to generalize.

3. Intuition

Overfitting: Think of a tree as a student memorizing the training answers instead of learning the concept. It looks perfect on practice (train data) but fails on exam (test data).

Unstable Splits: If your first question in 20 questions is different, the entire game changes. Similarly, a tiny dataset change shifts the root split, changing the entire tree.

Linear Relationships: Imagine drawing decision boundaries only with vertical and horizontal lines — approximating a diagonal line becomes jagged and inefficient.

Imbalanced Classes: If 95% of data is “Class A,” the tree can get lazy and predict “A” most of the time, ignoring the minority class.

Outliers: A single weird observation can pull a split in the wrong direction, making the tree chase noise instead of patterns.

Decision Trees and Their Optimization Criteria

Decision Trees are among the most fundamental machine learning models because they mimic human decision-making with “if-else” rules. The basic idea is to split the dataset into groups that are increasingly homogeneous in terms of the target variable.

In Classification problems, the split criterion focuses on “purity” of class labels in child nodes. Common criteria include:

Gini Index: A measure of how often a randomly chosen element would be misclassified if it was labeled according to the distribution of labels in a node.

Entropy / Information Gain: Measures uncertainty. A good split significantly reduces entropy.

In Regression problems, the focus is on reducing the variance of the response variable in child nodes.

Mean Squared Error (MSE) is often minimized. A good split ensures that each node has predictions that are close to the actual values.

Trees are non-parametric models, which means they don’t assume any underlying functional form between features and outcomes. This flexibility makes them attractive, but also risky, because they can easily overfit the data.

Bagging (Bootstrap Aggregating) and Random Forests

Bagging addresses one of the major weaknesses of Decision Trees — high variance. A single tree can look very different with small changes in the dataset, which reduces reliability. Bagging stabilizes predictions by training many trees on bootstrapped samples of the data and aggregating their predictions.

In regression, predictions are averaged across trees.

In classification, predictions are usually made by majority vote.

Random Forests add an additional layer of randomness: when splitting nodes, only a random subset of features is considered. This decorrelates the trees and makes the ensemble stronger.

Advantages:

High accuracy out-of-the-box with minimal tuning.

Robust against overfitting compared to a single tree.

Provides feature importance measures.

Limitations:

Interpretability is lost compared to a single tree.

Large ensembles can be computationally heavy.

They reduce variance but don’t necessarily reduce bias.

Boosting and Gradient Boosted Decision Trees (GBDT)

Boosting takes a very different approach from Bagging. Instead of training trees independently, Boosting trains trees sequentially. Each new tree focuses on correcting the errors made by the previous ones. Over time, the model shifts its attention toward the “hard-to-predict” data points.

Gradient Boosted Decision Trees (GBDT) formalize this process by fitting each new tree to the gradient of the loss function with respect to the model’s predictions. This makes boosting highly flexible — it can optimize almost any differentiable loss function.

Advantages:

Typically achieves higher accuracy than Bagging methods.

Can be tailored to different tasks through choice of loss function.

Learns complex patterns and interactions.

Limitations:

Much more sensitive to hyperparameter tuning (e.g., learning rate, tree depth, number of trees).

Computationally more expensive due to sequential training.

Can overfit if not carefully regularized.

Comparison: CART, Random Forest, and GBDT

CART (single tree): Simple, interpretable, but unstable and prone to overfitting.

Random Forest (Bagging): Reduces variance by averaging, gives strong baseline performance, good for general use.

GBDT (Boosting): Reduces bias and captures complex patterns, often delivers state-of-the-art results, but needs careful tuning and is more computationally costly.

Think of them this way:

CART = raw material.

Random Forest = stable, balanced product (variance reduced).

GBDT = refined, powerful but fragile product (bias reduced).

Other Popular Decision Tree–Based Algorithms

XGBoost: Optimized version of GBDT, adds regularization, efficient parallelization, and sparsity handling. Extremely popular in competitions.

LightGBM: Optimized for speed and large datasets, uses histogram-based splits and gradient-based sampling. Scales better to millions of rows.

CatBoost: Specialized for categorical features, handles them without preprocessing, avoids target leakage with innovative encoding.

ExtraTrees (Extremely Randomized Trees): Similar to Random Forest but with more randomness in choosing splits, often faster and reduces variance further.

These became popular because they take the theoretical strengths of trees and ensembles, but implement them in ways that handle real-world challenges: huge datasets, categorical variables, memory efficiency, and training speed.

BOOSTING as implemented in GBDT
Boosting is a technique designed to create a strong classifier by combining multiple weak classifiers. The process involves building models sequentially, where each new model aims to correct the errors made by the previous ones. Initially, a model is built using the training data. Subsequent models are then trained to address the mistakes of their predecessors. Boosting assigns weights to the data points in the original dataset. Instances that were misclassified by the previous model receive higher weights while those that were correctly classified receive lower weights. The subsequent model learns from the weighted dataset, focusing its attention on harder-to-learn examples (those with higher weights). This continues till the whole training dataset is accurately predicted, or a predefined maximum number of models is reached. In gradient boosting, at each step, a new weak model is trained to predict the "error" of the current strong model (which is called the pseudo response). The weak model (that is, the "error") is then added to the strong model with a negative sign to reduce the error of the strong model.  This operation repeats until a stopping criterion is met, such as a maximum number of iterations or if the (strong) model begins to overfit as measured on a separate validation dataset.
Suppose we use the same dataset as used above,
Initial weak learner: Predicts constant average value: ŷ₀ = 7.
Residuals (errors): r = y - ŷ₀ = [-5, -3, -1, 1, 3, 5]
Fit weak learner to residuals: 
Update model with learning rate 0.5: ŷ₁ = ŷ₀ + 0.5 * r̂
For X=5:
Initial prediction = 7
Residual model correction = +1.5
New prediction = 7 + 0.5*1.5 = 7.75
Residuals shrink further each round, prediction converges towards true value 10.

The performance of Boosting usually surpasses that of Bagging. Boosting can perform well even on imbalanced datasets. Unlike Bagging, which averages predictions, Boosting uses a weighted combination of weak learners, where later learners have more influence. This often yields stronger performance, especially on imbalanced or complex datasets. Bagging does not reduce bias much, since each tree may still be simplistic. Boosting reduces bias more effectively, since it iteratively learns from errors.

Topic: Optimization criteria used in Decision Tree and BAGGING
YourAnalysis:
To understand how a decision tree learns, it's all about how it chooses the best split at each step. The goal is always to make the resulting groups as homogenous as possible. For a classification task, the algorithm tries to maximize the purity of the new nodes, using criteria like Gini Impurity or Information Gain to reduce the mix of classes in each subgroup. For a regression task, the goal is instead to minimize prediction error. It does this by finding splits that result in the lowest possible Mean Squared Error within the new groups, which means the data points within each group end up being very similar in value.

A Random Forest is a powerful solution to the main weakness of a single decision tree, which is its tendency to overfit. It works by creating an ensemble, or forest, of many diverse trees using a process called BAGGING, which stands for Bootstrap Aggregating. It builds each tree on a slightly different random sample of the training data. Crucially, Random Forest also adds another layer of randomness: at each split, it only considers a random subset of the available features. This process of sampling both the data and the features creates a set of decorrelated trees. The final prediction is then made by aggregating the results of all trees, either through a majority vote for classification or by averaging for regression. This has the effect of canceling out the errors of individual trees, resulting in a single, robust, and highly accurate model.

Introduction:
A decision tree is a prediction model that looks like a branching flowchart: it starts from a single root and repeatedly splits the data into branches until terminal leaves give the final prediction or decision.
How splitting is chosen:
At each node the tree tests possible splits and scores each one with an objective that measures how much the split improves the node. The algorithm picks the split that gives the largest improvement and then repeats the process on the resulting child nodes until a stopping rule is met.
Classification — how node quality is measured:
Gini index: computed as 1 minus the sum of the squared proportions of each class in the node. A node is perfectly pure (Gini = 0) when all items belong to a single class; Gini grows as the class mix becomes more even.
Entropy: computed as the negative of the sum, over classes, of (class proportion multiplied by the base-2 logarithm of that proportion). Entropy measures uncertainty; equal class proportions give high entropy, a pure node gives zero.
When evaluating a split, the tree compares the impurity of the parent node with the weighted impurity of the child nodes; the split that reduces impurity the most is preferred. The reduction in entropy is often called information gain.
Regression — how node quality is measured:
Mean Squared Error (MSE): the average of the squared differences between each target value in the node and the node’s mean. Squaring emphasizes larger errors, so MSE is sensitive to outliers.
Mean Absolute Error (MAE): the average of the absolute differences between each target value and the node’s central value. MAE is less sensitive to outliers than MSE.
For regression splits, the tree selects the split that produces child nodes with the lowest combined error according to the chosen metric.
Why these measures are appropriate:
For classification, low impurity means child nodes contain mostly one class, which improves prediction clarity. For regression, low post-split error means predictions made using the child-node summaries (mean or median) will be more accurate. The greedy choice at each node pushes the tree toward partitions that are easier to predict.
Practical considerations:
Stopping rules and pruning: without limits a tree can grow very deep and overfit, so common controls are minimum samples per node, maximum tree depth, or pruning methods that remove branches with little validation benefit.
Overfitting vs interpretability: deep trees capture complex patterns but may overfit noise; shallow trees generalize better but can miss structure. Trees remain attractive because they are easy to interpret.
Choice of split criterion: Gini and entropy usually yield similar splits; choice rarely changes results dramatically. For regression, MSE is the default, while MAE is chosen when robustness to outliers is desired.
Simple analogy:
Imagine sorting marbles. If you sort by color (classification), a good split puts mostly one color in each container. If you sort by size (regression), a good split puts marbles of similar size together. The splitting criterion is the rule that tells you which cut produces more useful groups.
Conclusion:
Decision trees build a hierarchy of decisions by repeatedly choosing splits that improve a chosen measure: impurity reduction for classification or error reduction for regression. With appropriate stopping or pruning they are powerful, interpretable models suitable for many prediction tasks.

Topic: Advantages and limitations of CART, BAGGING (Random Forest), BOOSTING (GBDT) algorithms
YourAnalysis:
CART (Classification and Regression Trees) is one of the most fundamental algorithms in machine learning. Its biggest strength lies in its interpretability. A single decision tree is easy to visualize, and its rules can be directly explained to non-technical stakeholders, making it useful in fields where transparency is crucial, such as healthcare or policy-making. CART can also naturally handle both categorical and continuous data, as well as missing values. From a computational perspective, it is lightweight and relatively fast to train. However, its simplicity is also its weakness. CART trees are highly prone to overfitting, especially when allowed to grow deep. They are sensitive to small variations in the training set, often producing very different trees if the data is perturbed. Furthermore, their predictive accuracy is generally lower compared to modern ensemble methods, which has limited their usage as standalone models in high-stakes predictive tasks.

Bagging and Random Forest were introduced to overcome some of CART’s limitations. Bagging, short for bootstrap aggregating, reduces variance by training multiple trees on different bootstrapped samples and averaging their predictions. Random Forest takes this idea further by adding randomness in feature selection at each split, ensuring that individual trees are less correlated. The result is a model that is far more robust and accurate than a single decision tree. Random Forests handle high-dimensional data well, resist overfitting due to averaging, and provide a reliable measure of feature importance, which helps in understanding global patterns in data. However, this improvement comes at the cost of interpretability. Additionally, training and inference are more computationally intensive, especially with large datasets or a high number of trees.

Boosting, particularly Gradient Boosted Decision Trees (GBDT), takes a different approach. Instead of building trees independently, boosting builds them sequentially, where each new tree corrects the errors of the previous ones. This stage-wise optimization makes boosting highly powerful and capable of achieving state-of-the-art accuracy on structured datasets.  The main limitations of boosting are its sensitivity to noise and outliers, as well as its reliance on careful hyperparameter tuning. If parameters such as learning rate, number of trees, or maximum depth are not properly balanced, the model can either overfit or underfit. Boosting is also slower to train than bagging-based methods because of its sequential nature.

In summary, CART is valuable for simplicity and interpretability but limited in predictive power. Random Forest addresses these issues through ensemble averaging, making it robust and accurate at the cost of transparency. Boosting (GBDT) delivers the highest accuracy and flexibility but requires more computational resources and careful tuning. The choice among them depends on the problem context: if interpretability is key, CART is useful; if balanced performance and robustness are needed, Random Forest is a strong choice; and if maximum predictive power is the goal, GBDT is the most suitable.

Bagging (Bootstrap Aggregating) is a technique used in Random Forests to create a strong and stable model from many weaker models (decision trees). The steps are:
1. Bootstrapping the data: From the original dataset, multiple random samples are drawn with replacement, meaning some records may appear multiple times in a sample while others may be left out. Each such sample is the training set for one decision tree.
2. Training multiple trees: Each bootstrapped dataset is used to train a separate decision tree. Since the samples are different, the trees will also be different, even though they are trained on the same overall data distribution.
3. Aggregating predictions:
    * For classification, the final prediction is made by majority voting—the class chosen by most trees is selected.
    * For regression, the prediction is the average of all tree outputs.

Bagging is crucial because:
* Decision trees are prone to high variance (their predictions change a lot if the data changes slightly).
* Bagging reduces this variance because averaging over many diverse trees cancels out individual errors.
* This makes the Random Forest more robust, less overfitted, and more accurate than a single tree.

Topic: Optimization criteria used in Decision Tree - for regression and classification
YourAnalysis:
When a decision tree is constructed, the main challenge at each step is to decide the best place to split the data. This decision is not random; it is guided by optimization criteria. These criteria measure how “good” a particular split is, and they differ based on whether the problem at hand is classification or regression.

In the case of classification trees, the objective is to make the resulting nodes as pure as possible, meaning that most samples in a node belong to a single class. One of the most widely used measures here is the Gini Index. It calculates impurity based on the probabilities of different classes in a node. A node with all samples from one class has a Gini value of zero, which indicates perfect purity. If the data is more mixed, the Gini value increases, showing greater impurity. Because it is simple and fast to compute, CART (Classification and Regression Trees) often uses Gini as the default criterion. Another important measure is Entropy, which comes from information theory. Entropy calculates the amount of disorder in a node, being zero for pure nodes and higher for mixed ones. To select a  split, decision trees calculate the reduction  in entropy, known as Information Gain, and choose the split that gives the highest gain. Compared to Gini,entropy is slightly more computationally expensive  because it involves logarithms, but it provides a solid theoretical foundation.

Regression trees, on the other hand do  not deal  with classes but with continuous values such as prices or temperatures. Here, the aim is not purity but minimising prediction  errors. One way to evaluate splits is by looking at  Variance Reduction. If the variance of the target values decreases significantly after a split, it means the  child nodes are more consistent and the split is considered good. Another common measure is the Mean Squared Error (MSE), which  calculates the average squared difference  between actual values and predicted values  in a node. Since large errors are penalized more heavily by the squaring, MSE is a popular choice for guiding regression trees. There is also the Mean Absolute Error (MAE), which measures average absolute deviation from the predicted value. This method is more robust to outliers but less common than MSE because it is harder for trees to optimize mathematically.

To summarize, classification trees use criteria such as Gini Index and Entropy to focus on creating pure nodes, while regression trees use measures like Variance Reduction and MSE to reduce prediction errors. These optimization criteria are crucial because they directly influence how a decision tree grows and how well it generalizes to new, unseen data.

Boosting is an ensemble technique, that is used for both classification and regression. In a simple way, it builds a strong learner by combining many weak learners, usually decision trees. The idea is not to train all trees independently, but to train sequentially, where each new tree focuses on the errors done by the previous ones.
In class we saw that, in Gradient Boosted Decision Trees (GBDT), the training process is guided by gradient descent. Instead of directly fitting the target, each tree tries to fit the residual errors (the difference between actual values and predictions so far). Why? Because minimizing the loss function, step by step can be expressed as moving in the direction of the negative gradient. Hence, each new tree is effectively correcting the mistakes of the existing model.
Now, why gradients? Because loss functions can be complex, and calculating the exact solution may not be possible. Gradients give us a direction for improvement, just like in optimization problems. The process continues for many iterations, and the final prediction is the sum of all the weak learners weighted together.
One important detail is the learning rate, which controls how much each new tree contributes. A large rate can lead to overfitting, while a small rate requires more trees but usually generalizes better.
In short, boosting in GBDT is like a team effort where each decision tree learns from the mistakes of the previous ones. This makes it one of the most powerful and accurate methods in practice, used widely in competitions and real-world applications.

Another option is mean absolute error (MAE), which takes absolute deviations instead of squared deviations and is less sensitive to extreme outliers. The tree evaluates splits and chooses the one that minimizes error in the child nodes.

-> These criteria work because they match the goal of the task: in classification we want each branch to separate the classes as cleanly as possible, and in regression we want each branch to make predictions that are as accurate as possible. By repeatedly choosing splits that reduce impurity or minimize error, the tree organizes messy data into useful partitions.

If the task is sorting by size, a good split means each jar has marbles that are roughly the same size. The optimization criteria such as Gini, entropy, MSE, or MAE are the rules the child follows to decide which split makes the jars more organized, and step by step the sorting improves until the marbles are arranged in a way that makes sense.

Bagging, short for bootstrap aggregating, is the foundation of random forests. At its core, bagging is about creating diversity in models by manipulating the training data itself. Instead of training one model on the entire dataset, we repeatedly draw bootstrap samples—new datasets created by sampling with replacement from the original. Each of these samples has the same size as the original but looks slightly different: some points are duplicated, others are missing. A decision tree, which is highly sensitive to small changes in the data, is then trained on each bootstrap sample. When it comes time to predict, the ensemble does not rely on any single tree; instead, all the trees vote in classification tasks or average their outputs in regression tasks.

The strength of this technique lies in variance reduction. Decision trees alone are unstable and prone to overfitting; bagging tames this instability by averaging across many models. This does not eliminate bias, so if the base learner is systematically wrong, bagging will not fix it. What it does guarantee is a more stable, noise-resistant model, one less likely to chase random quirks of the training data. An added benefit is the out-of-bag error estimate, which serves as an internal validation check without requiring a separate holdout dataset.

Random forests extend bagging by adding another source of randomness—feature selection at each split. This prevents strong predictors from dominating every tree and reduces correlation among trees, which is critical because averaging highly correlated models provides little gain. By forcing diversity, random forests achieve stronger predictive power than plain bagging.

The limitation is that bagging and random forests trade interpretability for accuracy. Hundreds of bootstrapped trees form a powerful “black box,” but the cost is computational load and the loss of a clear, human-readable model. Despite this, the efficiency gains in variance reduction and generalization explain why bagging remains one of the most influential ensemble techniques in machine learning.
